title: ADO to ADO Migration in 2026: A Guide to Cross-Tenant Moves, Mergers, and Splits
summary:
Moving between Azure DevOps organizations or tenants? This guide covers moves, merges, and splits, what migrates, your options, and the five stages to run it. OpsHub Migrator for Microsoft Azure DevOps (OM4ADO) supports it with history, user identity mapping across tenants, and delta migration, so teams keep working.

TL;DR

Azure DevOps migration moves projects between organizations, tenants, or projects and can include merging several sources into one target or splitting one source into several targets. It covers work items with history, comments, attachments, and links, plus test plans, pipelines, repositories, dashboards, area and iteration paths, users, teams, and groups. Options include Microsoft's Data Migration Tool for Server-to-Services moves, a dedicated solution such as OM4ADO, or CSV export and import. The five stages are planning and scoping, mapping user identities, reconciling process templates, running a dry run with delta migration and cutover, and validating. A migration solution fits moves where history, traceability, and user identities must carry over while teams keep working.

Is it possible to migrate projects from one Azure DevOps organization to another?

Moving work from one Azure DevOps organization to another sounds like a copy job. It is not. The quick methods change work item IDs, reset dates, and drop links. A planned migration keeps the history, the relationships, and the people's work intact.

Azure DevOps to Azure DevOps migration moves projects between two Azure DevOps Services organizations, where both the source and the target are in the cloud. If your source is still on-premises (TFS or Azure DevOps Server), that is a different path, covered in our TFS to Azure DevOps guide.

The migration comes in three types of move:

  • Project to project: One or more team projects move into another organization.
  • Organization to organization: All projects of an organization move into a different organization.
  • Tenant to tenant: The target organization sits in a different Microsoft Entra ID tenant, so sign-in and user identities change along with the data. Any of these moves can also be a merge (several sources into one target) or a split (one source into several targets). Merges and splits have their own guides: How to merge Azure DevOps instances and How to split an Azure DevOps instance.

Why do teams move between Azure DevOps organizations?

A change in the business usually triggers the move:

  • Acquisition or consolidation: Two companies or business units want one shared home. This leads to a merge.
  • Divestiture or carve-out: A unit is sold or spun off and needs its own organization. This leads to a split.
  • Tenant change: A rebrand or IT consolidation moves the company to a different Microsoft Entra ID tenant. User identity mapping becomes the main task.
  • Moving off a trial or personal organization: Work started in a personal or trial organization needs a company-owned home.
  • Data residency or compliance: A rule about where data must live moves the organization.
  • Internal reorganization: Teams are regrouped, and the old project structure no longer fits. ## What are the options for an Azure DevOps to Azure DevOps migration?

Three approaches are available. Each fits a different kind of move.

Approach What it fits Points to consider
Microsoft Data Migration Tool Moving one Azure DevOps Server collection into a new Azure DevOps Services organization Microsoft documents it for Server to Services moves. Organization to organization is not among its scenarios.
A dedicated migration solution such as OM4ADO Moves where history, links, test assets, and user identities must carry over, and the source stays in use until cutover Set up through a graphical interface, with no code to write
CSV export and import Moving a list of work items between projects Microsoft documents only parent-child links on import. History is not carried over, and some fields (such as Effort) are ignored on import.

For a closer comparison, see our ADO migration tool guide.

What moves in an Azure DevOps to Azure DevOps migration

Most of your working data moves across with its history. One detail to know up front: Azure DevOps assigns new ID numbers to work items in the target and cannot reuse the original ones. A planned migration works around this by keeping each item's original ID as a reference and preserving its real dates and authorship, so the history stays intact. The table below shows what OM4ADO migrates.

Work items Standard and custom work items, with history, comments, attachments, inline images, and user mentions
Relationships Parent, child, and related links between work items
Test entities Test plans, test suites, test runs, and test results
Pipelines Build and release pipelines
Queries, dashboards, and widgets Queries, dashboards, and widgets, with their configuration
Area and iteration paths Area and iteration paths, mapped to the target
Users, teams, and groups Users, teams, and groups, with user identity mapping across tenants
Repositories Git repositories, and TFVC changesets with version history and changeset labels

For a full side-by-side comparison of every tool, read best Azure DevOps migration solutions in 2026.

Where does OM4ADO fit?

OpsHub Migrator for Microsoft Azure DevOps (OM4ADO) is a migration solution built for Azure DevOps and listed on the Microsoft marketplace. You set up the migration in a graphical interface, without writing code. It supports:

  • Selective project migration: Move only the projects you pick. If just 3 of your 40 projects need to go, move those 3 and leave the rest.
  • History and links preserved: Work items, test plans, pipelines, repositories, dashboards, queries, and area and iteration paths all come across with their history and their links intact.
  • User identity mapping across tenants: Match each source user to the right person in the target, even when the two sides sit in different Microsoft Entra ID tenants.
  • Delta migration that keeps the source live: Keep working in the source while the migration runs. OM4ADO keeps syncing new changes until you are ready to switch over.
  • Automatic failure retry and re-run from the last checkpoint: If something fails, the migration retries and carries on from the last checkpoint instead of running the whole thing again.
  • No volume limit: Move as much as you need, with no cap on the number of items. OM4ADO is purpose-built for Azure DevOps and listed on the Microsoft marketplace, and OpsHub has spent over two decades moving engineering data between systems without losing history or traceability.

How to plan and run the migration?

A migration runs in five stages.

  1. Plan and scope. List what you have and decide what moves. Old, closed projects are often better archived. You can migrate into a target that already has data. If you move only a subset, include the items it links to, so parent and child links are not orphaned.
  2. Map user identities. Inside one shared tenant, mapping is mostly automatic. Across tenants or domains, map identities explicitly so history and assignments land on the right people. Map only the identities you need and resolve any "unknown" identity before the real run.
  3. Reconcile process templates. The "Change process" option in Azure DevOps works only between processes that share a base model. Decide early whether the target keeps the source process or uses a different one, then map work item types, fields, and states during the migration.
  4. Dry run, delta migration, and cutover. Run the dry run into a test target first. For the real run, delta migration carries only what changed since the last pass. Freeze the source as read-only at the end, run one final delta, and cut over. Then recreate service connections and secrets, and point build agents at the new organization.
  5. Validate. Compare work item counts by type, repositories, and pipeline definitions. Spot-check history, dates, and links on a sample. Confirm that dashboards render and permissions match. For a worked example, watch the Azure DevOps cloud-to-cloud migration video.

What changes for a merge or a split of instances?

Merge: Two sources can carry the same work item IDs, area paths, or team names, and these collide in the shared target. Decide up front whether incoming teams become separate projects or separate teams in one project. Build and release history does not combine cleanly. See the merge guide.

Split: Move only the chosen parts without orphaning the links between them. For example, moving only active work items can leave their completed parents behind. See the split guide.

What are the most common Azure DevOps migration risks?

  • History is out of order: The run stops when a work item's revision dates are not in sequence. Use a solution that writes history in its original order.
  • Permission gaps: "Not authorized" errors appear partway through when the migration account lacks access. Use an account with full access to both source and target and check scopes first.
  • Process template mismatch: Field and work item type errors appear when the source and target templates differ. Reconcile work item types, fields, and states before migrating.
  • Broken link tracking: Parent, child, and related links do not resolve in the target when link tracking is set up incorrectly. Configure link tracking correctly or use a solution that manages it.
  • Notification flood: The migration can email the whole organization with system notifications. Control notification settings during the migration window.
  • ID or name collisions (merge): Two sources can use the same IDs, area paths, or team names, and they collide in the shared target. Plan the target structure before you move.
  • Orphaned links (split): Items lose the parents or children that stayed behind in the source. Include linked items in the scope. ### How do you recover from a partial failure?

A migration should retry the failed items and resume from where it stopped, without deleting what is already in the target. This way, a partial run is recoverable and not a loss.

Conclusion

The data is an easy part. What decides the outcome is whether history, relationships, and people's work arrive intact, and whether teams keep working during the move. Settle the target structure, map identities, reconcile process templates, prove the plan with a dry run, and validate against the source before cutover.

This page is part of our wider guide, How to migrate across the Azure DevOps ecosystem.

Frequently asked questions

Should I build my own migration or use a migration solution?

It depends on the size and the stakes of the move. Building it yourself is mostly a cost of engineer time: setup, scripts, identity mapping, process template work, and fixing failures. A migration solution takes on that work, including the failure handling. This table shows when each route fits.

Building it yourself fits when A migration solution fits when
The move is small You are moving many projects or many work items
Process templates are standard Process templates are customized and differ
Source and target share a tenant Source and target are in different tenants
Engineers know the Azure DevOps object model and have time History and traceability must survive for audit or reporting
A short outage is acceptable The source must stay in use during the move

AI assistants can speed up the first draft of a migration script, but the script still runs against production data, so it needs a review, and responsibility for the result stays with your team.

Can I migrate into an organization that already has data?

Yes. A target does not need to be empty, though a clean target makes validation simpler.

Does Microsoft offer a tool for organization-to-organization migration?

Microsoft's Data Migration Tool is documented for Azure DevOps Server to Azure DevOps Services moves. For organization to organization moves, teams use scripts or a dedicated migration solution such as OM4ADO.

How long does an Azure DevOps to Azure DevOps migration take?

The duration depends on four things: the volume of work items and repositories, Azure DevOps API rate limits, how different the source and target customizations are, and how much identity and process mapping is needed. A dry run on your own data gives the reliable timeline.

Can I merge several collections into one organization?

Yes, with OM4ADO. It can bring several source collections into one Azure DevOps organization. The full method is in the guide to merging multiple Azure DevOps or TFS instances.

For a plan mapped to your own Azure DevOps estate, and the complete detail on moves, merges, and splits, read the full guide here.

집에 NAS가 있다면 유튜브 쇼츠 자동화 시스템을 직접 구축할 수 있습니다. UGREEN DXP4800PLUS NAS에서 쇼츠 자동화 파이프라인을 구축한 과정을 살펴봅니다.

운영 상태를 확인할 항목

  • 수집 영상과 저장 스냅샷 수: 같은 조회 시각을 기록하고 집계
  • 성장률 계산: 비교 스냅샷이 없는 영상과 계산 실패를 구분
  • 콘텐츠 분류: 표본과 분류 조건을 함께 기록
  • 영상 생성: 대본·음성·자막의 결과를 단계별로 확인

수집 규모나 성공률을 인용하려면 집계 시각·질의·출력 원문을 함께 보관해야 합니다. 이 글에서는 근거를 함께 제시할 수 없는 수치 대신 구성과 확인 절차를 설명합니다. 다른 NAS 모델이나 버전에서는 동작을 별도로 확인하세요.

단순 성공 사례가 아닙니다. FastAPI 404 오류, 분류기 정확도 문제, 영상 생성 실패까지 실제 겪은 삽질과 해결 과정을 함께 담았습니다.

전체 파이프라인 구조

NAS에서는 YouTube API 수집부터 PostgreSQL 저장, 성장률·콘텐츠 분류, 대본·음성·영상 생성, drafts 저장까지를 독립된 서비스로 운영했습니다. Python 구현과 단계별 코드는 유튜브 쇼츠를 Python으로 자동 생성하는 방법에 정리했습니다. 같은 구현을 반복하기보다 DXP4800PLUS에서 확인한 운영 상태와 장애 해결에 초점을 맞춥니다.

FastAPI app.mount("/") 사용 시 API 404 오류 해결 방법

FastAPI에서 정적 파일을 루트(/)에 mount한 뒤 API가 404로 응답하는 문제를 실제로 겪었습니다. 원인은 루트 마운트가 뒤에 선언된 경로보다 먼저 요청을 가로채는 라우팅 순서였습니다. API 라우트를 먼저 등록하고 정적 파일 mount를 마지막에 두는 방식으로 해결했습니다. 재현 코드와 최소 예시는 FastAPI app.mount 사용 후 API가 404가 되는 이유와 해결 방법에 따로 정리했습니다.

YouTube 트렌드 수집기에서 AI 콘텐츠가 안 잡히는 이유

AI_AUTOMATION 클러스터에 필요한 영상이 충분히 수집되는지 먼저 확인합니다.

원인이 두 가지였습니다.

첫째, 수집 소스가 한국 급상승 위주였습니다. 한국 유튜브 급상승은 드라마, 연예, 뉴스가 압도적입니다. AI/IT 콘텐츠가 애초에 없었습니다.

아래 함수 이름은 수집 범위의 차이를 설명하기 위한 개념 예시이며 그대로 실행하는 완성 코드가 아닙니다.

# 기존: 한국 급상승과 쇼츠 검색
collect_popular(region="KR")  # 한국 급상승
collect_shorts_search(q="쇼츠")  # 한국 쇼츠

# 개선: 글로벌 키워드 + 채널 추가

collect_global_keywords(["ChatGPT shorts", "Claude AI", "n8n automation"])
collect_global_channels(["MKBHD", "Techquickie", "Linus Tech Tips"])

둘째, 분류기가 영어 키워드를 잡지 못했습니다. IT_DEVICE 클러스터를 새로 만들고 영어 키워드를 대폭 추가했습니다.

수집 범위를 바꾼 뒤에는 같은 집계 조건으로 분류별 영상 수를 비교하고, 실제로 관련 있는 영상인지 표본을 확인합니다.

왜 드라마 쇼츠는 자동화가 어렵고 IT 쇼츠는 쉬운가

자동 영상 생성을 처음 돌렸을 때 결과물이 처참했습니다. 트렌드 1위 드라마 쇼츠 대본으로 영상을 만들었는데, 배경에 여자 눈 클로즈업이 무한 루프로 돌아가고 자막은 음성과 전혀 맞지 않았습니다.

여기서 중요한 걸 배웠습니다.

IT 제품 스펙 비교 드라마/감정 연출
AI 도구 소개 연예/셀럽 가십

title: CloudWatch Omni Collects Azure Telemetry and Brings Different Metric Models Into One Space
summary:
TL;DR

  • CloudWatch Omni is the part of Amazon CloudWatch that holds logs, metrics and traces from several providers in one workspace, and it now collects four kinds of telemetry from Microsoft Azure.
  • The four kinds are Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network flow logs, and traces from Application Insights, all landed in CloudWatch and visible in Omni spaces.
  • Setup runs through a Microsoft Entra ID tenant connected to an AWS account and Region, and the collector is scoped by telemetry type, subscription, Azure Region, resource type and tag.
  • Collection is available from all Azure Public Regions and can be ingested into every Region where CloudWatch Omni runs, so the footprint follows the two providers' Region lists.
  • Azure platform metrics arrive at a one-minute collection frequency, are stored 93 days, and can be charted over 30 days at most on a single chart, so the retention a team sees in one console still follows each provider's rules.
  • Microsoft documents that pre-aggregated platform metrics and raw Prometheus metrics can report different values for the same sample time until latency settles and granularity matches, which is the reason thresholds need re-baselining after a migration.
  • The Entra tenant connection is a cross-cloud identity path, and it deserves a review of its own: who can change the connector, which subscriptions it can reach, and what it can read.

CloudWatch Omni now collects Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network flow logs and Application Insights traces. The announcement on 21 November 2026 frames the benefit simply: teams that run workloads on both clouds no longer need separate monitoring tools or custom pipelines to see their whole environment, and during an incident a slow request can be followed from an Azure-hosted service to its AWS dependencies without switching consoles.

That framing is accurate and it stops where the hard part begins. Bringing telemetry into one place simplifies collection and incident navigation. Microsoft's documentation describes the aggregation, granularity and latency that teams need to account for when comparing data and defining alerts.

The announcement page, which is where the telemetry types and the Entra ID tenant step are stated. Source: aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-cloudwatch-omni-microsoft-azure, captured 22 November 2026.

What the connector collects and what you choose

The list of collected signals is short enough to plan against: resource logs, platform metrics, flow logs from virtual networks, and traces from Application Insights.

The choices sit in the connector configuration. Connecting a tenant to an AWS account and Region opens a scope decision, and the post names the dimensions that scope it: telemetry types, subscriptions, Azure Regions, resource types and tags. Each of those is a filter that lets the team limit collection before enabling the connector.

Tags are the lever worth using first. A tag that already marks production workloads, cost centres or data classification turns the connector into a scoped collector and limits which Azure resources feed telemetry into CloudWatch.

The scope decision also sets the incident path. A connector limited to two subscriptions produces a dashboard that answers questions about those two, and the first incident that touches a third subscription will send someone back to the console to widen it under pressure. Writing that boundary down next to the alert rules is cheaper than discovering it at 3am.

Netics editorial visual, 22 November 2026: what the Azure-native view exposes on one side, and what the Omni space receives on the other.

Azure platform metrics are pre-aggregated in Azure Monitor and collected at one-minute frequency

Azure resources produce platform metrics without any configuration, and Microsoft documents the collection frequency as one minute unless a specific metric definition says otherwise. That frequency is the finest resolution a consumer of those metrics can rely on.

The frequency figure is worth carrying into the connector design. A dashboard that aggregates five-minute buckets on the AWS side and one-minute samples on the Azure side compares two different things, and the difference is invisible once both series are drawn on the same axis.

Azure Monitor stores platform metrics in pre-aggregated form. Platform metrics are pre-aggregated and stored in a time-series database, and Azure Monitor collects them at one-minute frequency unless a metric definition states otherwise. A team that assumes it is reading raw samples will compare it against a source that does report raw samples and find a mismatch that looks like an incident.

Microsoft's diagram of how metrics reach Azure Monitor and where they are read back: separate paths, separate query surfaces, one subscription's worth of resources. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, retrieved 22 November 2026.

A 93-day store with a 30-day chart window

Retention follows the source as well. Microsoft stores platform and custom metrics for 93 days, and its documentation adds a detail that matters for trend work: a single metrics chart can query at most 30 days of data, whatever the store holds.

Longer history needs a different path. The same documentation points at sending platform metrics to a Log Analytics workspace for long-term trending, which is a deliberate act with its own cost. Application Insights is a separate case again: log-based metrics inherit the retention of the underlying logs, described as 31 days to two years, while Application Insights logs are stored 90 days.

A cross-cloud dashboard inherits all of this. A quarter-over-quarter capacity comparison built on Azure platform metrics needs a workspace export, whatever console displays it.

Netics editorial visual, 22 November 2026: the four numbers that decide what a cross-cloud comparison can honestly claim.

Two metric models in one space

The clearest warning in Microsoft's documentation is about sources. Metrics from different sources and collection methods can use different aggregations, and differences in aggregation and latency can lead to different metric values for a specific sample time. The same page says the differences disappear over time once latency stops being an issue and the comparison happens at the same granularity.

That single paragraph describes the working method for anyone assembling a cross-cloud view. Compare at the same granularity, allow for the ingest delay, and record which aggregation each alert depends on. Latency expectations for platform metrics exported through diagnostic settings are documented separately, so teams should review them before defining alert timing.

Dimensions add a second variable. Azure describes a namespace as a category for a metric and dimensions as name and value pairs that carry context, such as a disk-space metric whose Drive dimension separates C: from D:. Dimension names and values are case-insensitive. A cross-cloud query that groups by a dimension has to know which dimension names exist on the Azure side, since the equivalent in an AWS namespace is a different string even when the concept is identical.

The Azure Monitor metrics documentation, the page that carries the one-minute frequency, the 93-day store and the aggregation warning quoted here. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, captured 22 November 2026.

Re-baselining thresholds before the first alert

Every threshold that arrives with an existing alert rule was tuned against one source's aggregation and one source's latency. Evaluating the same threshold in a shared space requires checking its aggregation, granularity and latency first.

The practical order is short. List the alerts that will read cross-cloud data. For each, write down the source metric, its aggregation, and its granularity. Then re-derive the threshold from a period that includes a normal week and a deploy, and only then point the alert at the new space. Keep the remaining alerts on their source platform and schedule their recalculation.

Microsoft's Metrics explorer screenshot shows multiple metrics over time; the documentation separately warns that sources and collection methods may use different aggregations.

The Metrics explorer with an aggregation chosen per metric, which is the control that makes two charts comparable or not. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, retrieved 22 November 2026.

The Entra tenant connection as a trust path to review

Connecting a Microsoft Entra ID tenant to an AWS account and Region creates a relationship that outlives the project that motivated it. It is also the part of this feature a security review should read first.

Three questions belong in that review. Which identity in the AWS account can create, modify or remove the connector, since that identity now controls what telemetry crosses the boundary. Which subscriptions the connector can reach, because a wide scope reads more than the incident that started the work. And what the collected data contains, since resource logs and flow logs carry IP addresses, resource names and, depending on the workload, more than an operations team expects.

The review prevents a risky cross-cloud observability pattern: one connector, created during a pilot, with an unchanged scope, feeding a dashboard that becomes the shared view of both clouds. Teams that already run monitoring built around incidents will recognise the shape, and the fix is the same discipline applied to a new data source.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

Azure platform metrics are pre-aggregated in Azure Monitor and collected at one-minute frequency

Azure resources produce platform metrics without any configuration, and Microsoft documents the collection frequency as one minute unless a specific metric definition says otherwise. That frequency is the finest resolution a consumer of those metrics can rely on.

The frequency figure is worth carrying into the connector design. A dashboard that aggregates five-minute buckets on the AWS side and one-minute samples on the Azure side compares two different things, and the difference is invisible once both series are drawn on the same axis.

Azure Monitor stores platform metrics in pre-aggregated form. Platform metrics are pre-aggregated and stored in a time-series database, and Azure Monitor collects them at one-minute frequency unless a metric definition states otherwise. A team that assumes it is reading raw samples will compare it against a source that does report raw samples and find a mismatch that looks like an incident.

Microsoft's diagram of how metrics reach Azure Monitor and where they are read back: separate paths, separate query surfaces, one subscription's worth of resources. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, retrieved 22 November 2026.

A 93-day store with a 30-day chart window

Retention follows the source as well. Microsoft stores platform and custom metrics for 93 days, and its documentation adds a detail that matters for trend work: a single metrics chart can query at most 30 days of data, whatever the store holds.

Longer history needs a different path. The same documentation points at sending platform metrics to a Log Analytics workspace for long-term trending, which is a deliberate act with its own cost. A cross-cloud dashboard inherits all of this. A quarter-over-quarter capacity comparison built on Azure platform metrics needs a workspace export, whatever console displays it.

Netics editorial visual, 22 November 2026: the four numbers that decide what a cross-cloud comparison can honestly claim.

The clearest warning in Microsoft's documentation is about sources. Dimensions add a second variable. Azure describes a namespace as a category for a metric and dimensions as name and value pairs that carry context, such as a disk-space metric whose Drive dimension separates C: from D:. Dimension names and values are case-insensitive. A cross-cloud query that groups by a dimension has to know which dimension names exist on the Azure side, since the equivalent in an AWS namespace is a different string even when the concept is identical.

The Azure Monitor metrics documentation, the page that carries the one-minute frequency, the 93-day store and the aggregation warning quoted here. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, captured 22 November 2026.

Re-baselining thresholds before the first alert

Every threshold that arrives with an existing alert rule was tuned against one source's aggregation and one source's latency. Evaluating the same threshold in a shared space requires checking its aggregation, granularity and latency first.

The practical order is short. List the alerts that will read cross-cloud data. For each, write down the source metric, its aggregation, and its granularity. Then re-derive the threshold from a period that includes a normal week and a deploy, and only then point the alert at the new space. Keep the remaining alerts on their source platform and schedule their recalculation.

Microsoft's Metrics explorer screenshot shows multiple metrics over time; the documentation separately warns that sources and collection methods may use different aggregations.

The Metrics explorer with an aggregation chosen per metric, which is the control that makes two charts comparable or not. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, retrieved 22 November 2026.

The Entra tenant connection as a trust path to review

Connecting a Microsoft Entra ID tenant to an AWS account and Region creates a relationship that outlives the project that motivated it. It is also the part of this feature a security review should read first.

Three questions belong in that review. Which identity in the AWS account can create, modify or remove the connector, since that identity now controls what telemetry crosses the boundary. Which subscriptions the connector can reach, because a wide scope reads more than the incident that started the work. And what the collected data contains, since resource logs and flow logs carry IP addresses, resource names and, depending on the workload, more than an operations team expects.

The review prevents a risky cross-cloud observability pattern: one connector, created during a pilot, with an unchanged scope, feeding a dashboard that becomes the shared view of both clouds. Teams that already run monitoring built around incidents will recognise the shape, and the fix is the same discipline applied to a new data source.

title: AWS Savings Plans for startups: how much to commit and which plan
summary:
In short:

  • Compute Savings Plans give up to 66% off EC2, Fargate and Lambda; EC2 Instance Savings Plans up to 72% off one instance family; Database Savings Plans up to 35% off managed databases.
  • Commit to about 70 to 80% of your lowest steady hourly spend, not your average. Unused commitment is money you pay for nothing.
  • Fix waste first, then commit. A Savings Plan on an oversized server locks in the oversize.

A Savings Plan is the biggest single discount on AWS that needs no engineering work. You promise to spend a fixed amount per hour for one or three years, and AWS bills the matching usage at a lower rate. For a startup with a steady base of servers, that is often 25 to 40% off the biggest line of the bill.

It is also the easiest way to waste money on AWS. A commitment cannot be cancelled. Commit too much, or commit before you clean up, and you pay for capacity you do not use, every hour, for a year.

This post covers which plan to buy, how to size the commitment from your own data, and the order to do it in.

The three kinds of Savings Plans

Plan Covers Maximum discount Flexibility
Compute Savings Plans EC2 (any family, size, region, OS), Fargate, Lambda up to 66% High: follows you if you change instance types or move to containers
EC2 Instance Savings Plans One instance family in one region, e.g. m7g in us-east-1 up to 72% Low: tied to that family
Database Savings Plans Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream, DMS up to 35% Medium: any of these services, 1-year only

Sources: Compute and EC2 Instance Savings Plans and the Database Savings Plans announcement (December 2025).

The "maximum" numbers are for 3-year, all-upfront plans on specific instance types. A 1-year, no-upfront Compute Savings Plan typically lands around 25 to 30% off on-demand for common instances. For example, an m8gn.large in us-east-1 lists at about $0.146 an hour on-demand and about $0.106 with a 1-year no-upfront Compute Savings Plan, roughly 27% less (Holori price data).

Database Savings Plans are the new one. Before them, the only discount for RDS was a Reserved Instance tied to one engine, size and region. The new plan follows your database spend across services and sizes, which suits a startup that may resize or move from RDS to Aurora during the year.

Step 1: clean up before you commit

A Savings Plan discounts what you run. If what you run is oversized, you lock in the oversize for a year. Before buying, do the free fixes:

  • Delete idle resources and old environments: see 3 hidden AWS charges.
  • Right-size servers whose CPU sits below 20%.
  • Move what you can to Graviton, which is about 20% cheaper on its own: see moving to AWS Graviton.
  • Schedule dev and staging to stop at night and at weekends.

Then wait two to four weeks for usage to settle. The new, lower baseline is what you commit to.

Step 2: find your steady hourly floor

Savings Plans are bought in dollars per hour of discounted usage. The safe size comes from the lowest level your compute spend reaches, not the average.

The quickest way to see it is in Cost Explorer: filter to EC2 compute, Fargate and Lambda, set granularity to Hourly (it covers the last 14 days), and look for the floor of the line, usually at night or at weekends. If the floor is $4.00 an hour on-demand, that is your starting point.

AWS also recommends a commitment from your history:

aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation \
  --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP \
  --term-in-years ONE_YEAR \
  --payment-option NO_UPFRONT \
  --lookback-period-in-days THIRTY_DAYS \
  --query 'SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendation.SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendationDetails[0].[HourlyCommitmentToPurchase,EstimatedMonthlySavingsAmount,EstimatedAverageUtilization]'

Treat that number as an upper limit. The recommendation assumes the next year looks like the last 30 days. For a startup, it often does not.

Step 3: size the commitment

A rule that works for most startups: commit to 70 to 80% of the steady floor, in on-demand terms, converted to the discounted rate.

Example: the floor is $4.00 an hour on-demand, and the plan saves about 28%.

  • 75% of the floor is $3.00 an hour of on-demand usage.
  • At 28% off, that usage costs $2.16 an hour under the plan. That is the commitment.
  • Monthly: $2.16 × 730 hours = about $1,577, covering usage that would have cost $2,190 on-demand. Saving: about $613 a month, $7,350 a year.

Everything above $3.00 an hour of usage stays on-demand. That is not waste; it is the flexibility to shrink, change architecture, or move to Graviton later without paying for nothing.

If your usage grows, buy a second plan later. Several small plans bought over time are safer than one big plan bought at the start.

Step 4: pick the plan for each part of the bill

Situation Plan
EC2, ECS on Fargate or Lambda, still changing Compute Savings Plan, 1 year, no upfront
A big, stable EC2 fleet on one family you will not change EC2 Instance Savings Plan, for that family only
RDS or Aurora running all the time Database Savings Plan, 1 year
A database you plan to replace or shut down within a year Nothing yet, stay on-demand

Two things to check with databases:

  • Existing RDS Reserved Instances keep applying until they expire. Plan the Database Savings Plan for when they end, not on top of them.
  • Serverless databases (Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB on-demand) are covered too, so steady serverless spend can be committed like provisioned instances.

Step 5: watch utilisation every month

After buying, two numbers in Cost Explorer > Savings Plans tell you whether it was the right size:

  • Utilisation: how much of your commitment you used. Below about 95% means you committed too much.
  • Coverage: how much of your eligible usage the plans covered. Low coverage with high utilisation means there is room for another small plan.

Add a budget alert so a drop shows up the week it happens, not at the end of the year. In AWS Budgets, choose Create budget, then Savings Plans budget, then Utilization, set the threshold to 95% and add your email. It takes two minutes and needs no code.

You can also read both numbers from the command line for last month:

aws ce get-savings-plans-utilization \
  --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 \
  --query 'Total.Utilization.UtilizationPercentage'

aws ce get-savings-plans-coverage \
  --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 \
  --query 'SavingsPlansCoverages[].Coverage.CoveragePercentage'

Mistakes that waste money

  • Committing to the average, not the floor. Every quiet hour below the commitment is paid for and unused.
  • Buying 3 years because the discount is bigger. For a startup, the risk of change is bigger than the extra discount.
  • Buying an EC2 Instance Savings Plan, then moving to Graviton or containers. The plan stays on the old family.
  • Buying before cleaning up. The commitment locks in today's waste.
  • Forgetting the end date. When a plan expires, usage goes back to on-demand prices silently. Put the renewal date in a calendar.

Savings Plans checklist

  1. Clean up idle resources, right-size and move to Graviton first.
  2. Wait for usage to settle, then find the steady hourly floor.
  3. Commit to 70 to 80% of the floor, 1 year, no upfront.
  4. Use Compute Savings Plans for changing compute, Database Savings Plans for steady databases.
  5. Check utilisation and coverage monthly, and set a utilisation budget alert.
  6. Add small plans over time instead of one big one.

Want a rough idea of the total saving first? Try the AWS savings estimator. If you would like someone to size the commitment from your real usage, the AWS cost optimization review does exactly that, or start with a Free AWS Review.

Discount figures are from the AWS Savings Plans pricing page and the Database Savings Plans announcement, checked in November 2026. This is general information, not financial advice for your company.

Common questions

Which AWS Savings Plan is best for a startup?

Usually a 1-year, no-upfront Compute Savings Plan. It applies to EC2 in any family and region, Fargate and Lambda, so it keeps working when your architecture changes. The extra discount of an EC2 Instance Savings Plan only pays off if you are sure of the instance family for the whole term.

How much should I commit to?

Look at your hourly compute spend over the last 30 to 60 days and find the steady floor, the level you never go below. Commit to about 70 to 80% of that floor. Anything above it stays on-demand, which is fine.

What are Database Savings Plans?

A Savings Plan launched in December 2025 that gives up to 35% off Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream and DMS for a 1-year commitment with no upfront payment. Unlike Reserved Instances, it is not tied to one instance size or engine.

Can I cancel or sell a Savings Plan?

No. You pay the hourly commitment for the whole term, whether you use it or not. That is why the commitment should be smaller than your steady usage.

Should I pick 1 year or 3 years?

Most startups should pick 1 year. Three years gives a bigger discount, but your product, team and architecture will probably look very different in three years.

title: Running a Node.js API and a worker together
summary:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post.

A reliable setup for a Node.js API and a worker has four parts: both processes deploy from one repository so they never run different versions, a crash or memory leak in the worker cannot take down the API, the queue lives in a managed database with backups, and a bad release rolls back before most users see it. The cheapest version of that keeps the worker small and lets the API stop costing money while it is idle. On Gregale you describe the API and the worker in a Compose file and deploy them as one project with a managed PostgreSQL database. The API pauses between requests and is not billed while paused, and every production release reaches 1% of traffic first and rolls back on its own on errors (in beta). On raw machine price alone, Fly.io's smallest Machines cost less; the comparison below shows each option.

The API and the worker on Gregale 

# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    command: node dist/server.js
    ports: ['3000:3000']
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  worker:
    build: .
    command: node dist/worker.js
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:17

gregale deploy reads this as one project:

  • api becomes an app with a public URL. It pauses about a second after its last request and is not billed while paused.
  • worker has no ports:, so it becomes a background service that runs all the time.
  • db becomes a managed PostgreSQL database, and both services get its connection string as DATABASE_URL.
  • depends_on on api holds each new worker release until the API's release from the same deploy is live. If the API's release fails, the worker's release fails too and the current one keeps serving, so the two never run mixed versions.

To run migrations before each release, add a Compose step that the API waits for with condition: service_completed_successfully; Gregale runs it as the API's release command. A project with two or more services needs Hobby or higher. See Deploy a multi-service app and Deploy an Express app.

Where the worker gets its jobs

  • Postgres-backed, such as pg-boss or Graphile Worker: jobs live in the database you already have, covered by its backups and point-in-time restore. One less system to run, which suits most small apps.
  • Redis-backed, such as BullMQ: higher throughput, one more system to run. Gregale's managed Redis is not generally available yet, so point REDIS_URL at a Redis you run elsewhere.

Scheduled work does not need the worker either: a cron calls a path on your API on a schedule, and Gregale wakes the API for it.

gregale-dev/node-api-worker is a complete Compose project for this setup, with an Express API, a private worker and a job queue in Postgres. The worker has no polling loop: the API calls its private POST /drain after storing a job, so the worker runs only while there's work, and gregale deploy --project deploys all of it.

What two small always-on processes cost

The API and the worker each at the smallest paid size that stays on, before any database. Prices are each vendor's own, checked on November 25, 2026:

Platform API + worker, smallest always-on size Notes
Fly.io 2 × $2.19 = $4.38 a month (256 MB each) Lowest-priced regions; Fly.io Managed Postgres from $4 a month
Railway $5 a month minimum, credited toward usage Two services holding 256 MB each use about $5 of memory a month, before CPU
Gregale Gregale Hobby: $10 a month for 5 apps Includes 1 managed PostgreSQL database; the API is not billed while paused
DigitalOcean App Platform 2 × $5 = $10 a month (512 MiB each) The free tier covers static sites only
Render 2 × $7 = $14 a month (512 MB each) Workers have no free instance; Render Postgres from $6 a month
Heroku 2 × $7 = $14 a month (0.5 GB each, Basic) Eco dynos are $5 a month but sleep after 30 minutes idle

On Gregale, Hobby includes 200 GB-RAM-hours a month. A worker that runs all month at 256 MB uses most of it; an API that serves requests some of the time adds little, because paused time is not billed. Past the allowance, usage costs $0.05 per GB-RAM-hour, up to a spend cap you set, so a bill never runs past the limit you chose.

Reliability is where the platforms differ

  • Releases: Render, Railway and Heroku switch all traffic to a new version once it passes its health check, and rolling back is a manual step. Fly.io replaces Machines one at a time. Gregale sends 1% of the API's traffic first and rolls back on its own on a higher 5xx rate, crash loops or slower responses (in beta).
  • Version skew: on any platform, deploying the API and the worker separately can leave them on different versions for a while. Gregale's depends_on gate keeps them in step.
  • Database recovery: Gregale's managed PostgreSQL keeps a 7-day point-in-time restore window, and on paid plans a rollback can restore the database to the moment before a migration. A database runs in a single zone, with no high-availability promise.
  • Isolation: each Gregale app instance runs in its own Firecracker microVM, so a runaway worker cannot take memory from the API.

How to choose

  • Lowest price for two always-on processes, and you will configure Machines yourself: Fly.io.
  • Pay only for what each service uses, with Redis one click away: Railway.
  • A fixed price per instance on a familiar platform: Render or DigitalOcean App Platform.
  • A small team that wants the API and worker to release together, roll back on their own and stop billing for the API while it is idle: Gregale.

Sources

Gregale figures come from the plans and managed PostgreSQL docs. Other platforms' figures were checked against each vendor's own pages on November 25, 2026: Fly.io pricing, Fly.io Managed Postgres, Railway pricing, DigitalOcean App Platform pricing, Render pricing, Render free instances, Heroku pricing.

FAQ

What is the cheapest reliable way to run a Node.js API and a worker?

Two small processes from one repository, a queue in a managed database, and releases that keep both on the same version. On raw machine price Fly.io is cheapest, at $2.19 a month per 256 MB Machine. Gregale Hobby is $10 a month for both plus a managed PostgreSQL database, with the API unbilled while idle and automatic rollback (in beta).

Do I need Redis for a Node.js job queue?

Only for Redis-based queues such as BullMQ. pg-boss and Graphile Worker keep jobs in Postgres, so the database you already have, and its backups, cover the queue too.

Can the API and the worker deploy together on Gregale?

Yes. Describe both in a Compose file and deploy them as one project on Hobby or higher. With depends_on and condition: service_healthy, the worker's new release waits for the API's and fails with it, so the two never run mixed versions.
