event_model_payload.summary:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post.

A reliable setup for a Node.js API and a worker has four parts: both processes deploy from one repository so they never run different versions, a crash or memory leak in the worker cannot take down the API, the queue lives in a managed database with backups, and a bad release rolls back before most users see it. The cheapest version of that keeps the worker small and lets the API stop costing money while it is idle. On Gregale you describe the API and the worker in a Compose file and deploy them as one project with a managed PostgreSQL database. The API pauses between requests and is not billed while paused, and every production release reaches 1% of traffic first and rolls back on its own on errors (in beta). On raw machine price alone, Fly.io's smallest Machines cost less; the comparison below shows each option.

The API and the worker on Gregale 

# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    command: node dist/server.js
    ports: ['3000:3000']
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  worker:
    build: .
    command: node dist/worker.js
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:17

gregale deploy reads this as one project:

  • api becomes an app with a public URL. It pauses about a second after its last request and is not billed while paused.
  • worker has no ports:, so it becomes a background service that runs all the time.
  • db becomes a managed PostgreSQL database, and both services get its connection string as DATABASE_URL.
  • depends_on on api holds each new worker release until the API's release from the same deploy is live. If the API's release fails, the worker's release fails too and the current one keeps serving, so the two never run mixed versions.

To run migrations before each release, add a Compose step that the API waits for with condition: service_completed_successfully; Gregale runs it as the API's release command. A project with two or more services needs Hobby or higher. See Deploy a multi-service app and Deploy an Express app.

Where the worker gets its jobs

  • Postgres-backed, such as pg-boss or Graphile Worker: jobs live in the database you already have, covered by its backups and point-in-time restore. One less system to run, which suits most small apps.
  • Redis-backed, such as BullMQ: higher throughput, one more system to run. Gregale's managed Redis is not generally available yet, so point REDIS_URL at a Redis you run elsewhere.

Scheduled work does not need the worker either: a cron calls a path on your API on a schedule, and Gregale wakes the API for it.

gregale-dev/node-api-worker is a complete Compose project for this setup, with an Express API, a private worker and a job queue in Postgres. The worker has no polling loop: the API calls its private POST /drain after storing a job, so the worker runs only while there's work, and gregale deploy --project deploys all of it.

What two small always-on processes cost

The API and the worker each at the smallest paid size that stays on, before any database. Prices are each vendor's own, checked on November 25, 2026:

Platform API + worker, smallest always-on size Notes
Fly.io 2 × $2.19 = $4.38 a month (256 MB each) Lowest-priced regions; Fly.io Managed Postgres from $4 a month
Railway $5 a month minimum, credited toward usage Two services holding 256 MB each use about $5 of memory a month, before CPU
Gregale Gregale Hobby: $10 a month for 5 apps Includes 1 managed PostgreSQL database; the API is not billed while paused
DigitalOcean App Platform 2 × $5 = $10 a month (512 MiB each) The free tier covers static sites only
Render 2 × $7 = $14 a month (512 MB each) Workers have no free instance; Render Postgres from $6 a month
Heroku 2 × $7 = $14 a month (0.5 GB each, Basic) Eco dynos are $5 a month but sleep after 30 minutes idle

On Gregale, Hobby includes 200 GB-RAM-hours a month. A worker that runs all month at 256 MB uses most of it; an API that serves requests some of the time adds little, because paused time is not billed. Past the allowance, usage costs $0.05 per GB-RAM-hour, up to a spend cap you set, so a bill never runs past the limit you chose.

Reliability is where the platforms differ

  • Releases: Render, Railway and Heroku switch all traffic to a new version once it passes its health check, and rolling back is a manual step. Fly.io replaces Machines one at a time. Gregale sends 1% of the API's traffic first and rolls back on its own on a higher 5xx rate, crash loops or slower responses (in beta).
  • Version skew: on any platform, deploying the API and the worker separately can leave them on different versions for a while. Gregale's depends_on gate keeps them in step.
  • Database recovery: Gregale's managed PostgreSQL keeps a 7-day point-in-time restore window, and on paid plans a rollback can restore the database to the moment before a migration. A database runs in a single zone, with no high-availability promise.
  • Isolation: each Gregale app instance runs in its own Firecracker microVM, so a runaway worker cannot take memory from the API.

How to choose

  • Lowest price for two always-on processes, and you will configure Machines yourself: Fly.io.
  • Pay only for what each service uses, with Redis one click away: Railway.
  • A fixed price per instance on a familiar platform: Render or DigitalOcean App Platform.
  • A small team that wants the API and worker to release together, roll back on their own and stop billing for the API while it is idle: Gregale.

Sources

Gregale figures come from the plans and managed PostgreSQL docs. Other platforms' figures were checked against each vendor's own pages on November 25, 2026: Fly.io pricing, Fly.io Managed Postgres, Railway pricing, DigitalOcean App Platform pricing, Render pricing, Render free instances, Heroku pricing.

FAQ

What is the cheapest reliable way to run a Node.js API and a worker?

Two small processes from one repository, a queue in a managed database, and releases that keep both on the same version. On raw machine price Fly.io is cheapest, at $2.19 a month per 256 MB Machine. Gregale Hobby is $10 a month for both plus a managed PostgreSQL database, with the API unbilled while idle and automatic rollback (in beta).

Do I need Redis for a Node.js job queue?

Only for Redis-based queues such as BullMQ. pg-boss and Graphile Worker keep jobs in Postgres, so the database you already have, and its backups, cover the queue too.

Can the API and the worker deploy together on Gregale?

Yes. Describe both in a Compose file and deploy them as one project on Hobby or higher. With depends_on and condition: service_healthy, the worker's new release waits for the API's and fails with it, so the two never run mixed versions.

title: Web-Based vs Desktop SSH Clients: 8 Tools and Which Is Safer
summary:
For production servers, a desktop SSH client is the safer default. Your private key stays on your computer, and nothing new listens on the server.

Most web-based tools put a gateway or panel between your browser and the server, and that layer holds your keys or can open a shell. Keep one web path as a locked-down backup.

TL;DR

  • Desktop clients (CtrlOps, Termius, PuTTY, MobaXterm, SecureCRT) connect straight to the server. Your key stays on your device (Termius can also sync an encrypted copy).
  • Web-based tools (a web SSH gateway, or a panel like Coolify, aaPanel or Webmin) open the shell for you, and Coolify stores your private keys.
  • If you also want server tools with no web panel, server agent or cloud sync, CtrlOps does this in one desktop app. It covers files, monitoring, deploys, Docker and a security audit.

I made a short video on the same question:

What is a desktop SSH client and how does it work?

A desktop SSH client is an app on your computer that opens the SSH connection straight to the server. The private key stays on your disk, in your OS keychain or on a hardware key. The server needs only its normal SSH service.

your computer (app + key) --SSH--> your server

The simplest desktop client is the ssh command from OpenSSH (10.6, October 2026). It works in the macOS Terminal and installs as a package on Linux. On Windows 10 (build 1809 and later) and Windows 11, it is available as an optional feature. Keys live in ~/.ssh/ by default.

GUI clients such as CtrlOps, Termius, PuTTY, MobaXterm and SecureCRT work the same way and add saved sessions and other tools.

The trade-off: you install the app on each computer, and each person connects with their own keys, so a team gets no single login page.

What is a web-based SSH client and how does it work?

A web-based SSH client gives you a terminal in a browser tab, so yes, you can SSH from a browser. A browser cannot open raw SSH connections, so a server in the middle talks HTTPS or WebSocket to the browser and SSH to the server.

browser --HTTPS/WebSocket--> gateway or panel --SSH--> your server

There are three kinds:

  • A web SSH gateway: a web app, hosted by you, a vendor or a cloud provider, opens the SSH connection and shows the terminal.
  • A server panel with a terminal page: Coolify, aaPanel and Webmin open a shell after you log in. Strictly, they are panels, not SSH clients.
  • An in-browser client: the SSH client runs inside the page, as in ssheasy. Its site says no credentials are shared with its servers, which only tunnel the packets.

For a longer comparison, see these 7 key differences between web-based and local SSH clients.

How do the 8 tools compare?

Desktop apps keep keys on your computer by default; web panels run on your server:

Tool Type Where your keys or logins live Installed on your server? Synced to a vendor cloud? Free option
CtrlOps Desktop app (Mac, Windows, Linux) On your computer: saved servers and passwords AES-256 encrypted; a key file you pick stays where it is No agent No, on any plan Yes, 2 servers
Termius Desktop and mobile app On your device; paid plans also sync an end-to-end encrypted vault No Paid plans (keys can stay local) Yes, Starter
PuTTY Desktop app (Windows) Sessions in the Windows Registry; keys in .ppk files; no saved passwords No No Yes, free
MobaXterm Desktop app (Windows) Sessions in MobaXterm.ini; saved passwords behind a master password No No Yes, Home (12 sessions)
SecureCRT Desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux), plus iOS On your computer: local config files, encrypted saved passwords, optional configuration passphrase, local key files No None described; you export and import sessions No, 30-day trial
Coolify Self-hosted app platform with a web terminal On the Coolify server: encrypted in its database, plus key files Yes No, when self-hosted Yes, self-hosted
aaPanel Hosting panel with a terminal No key for its own server; for other servers, its docs do not say if it saves your password or key Yes Not stated Yes, free edition
Webmin System admin panel with a terminal No SSH key: the Webmin login opens a shell on its own server Yes No Yes, free

Which desktop SSH clients keep your keys on your computer?

CtrlOps, Termius, PuTTY, MobaXterm and SecureCRT all keep your private keys on your computer by default. CtrlOps has no cloud sync on any plan, and Termius syncs an encrypted vault only on paid plans.

1. CtrlOps: a local-first desktop app for server management

CtrlOps is a local-first desktop app for AI-assisted Linux server management.

It runs on Mac (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows (Microsoft Store), and Linux (Ubuntu 22.04+ and Debian 12+). Version 2.0.0 came out on 14 November 2026. It needs no agent on your servers.

"The fact that I don't need to install any agent on my servers sold me immediately."

  • Srushti Vasani, Product Hunt review

Where your keys live: on your computer, never on a CtrlOps server. Saved servers and remembered passwords are AES-256 encrypted on disk. The key that unlocks them sits in your OS keychain when available, with a copy in the app's storage. A key file you pick stays where it is (for example, ~/.ssh/), and CtrlOps saves only its path.

Optional Vault Lock asks for a passphrase at every start. Your servers and keys never sync to a cloud, and the privacy policy says your credentials, SSH keys, commands and logs never reach CtrlOps. Details: where CtrlOps stores your SSH keys and what it encrypts.

Key features

  • AI terminal: each terminal command the AI writes waits until you click Run.
  • File manager: uploads, downloads and edits over your SSH connection.
  • Live monitoring: no agent, refreshed every 2 seconds.
  • One-click deployment: Node.js, React, Next.js and static builds from GitHub.
  • Docker management: containers and Compose over SSH, with no Docker socket on the internet.
  • Security audit: 25 read-only audits over SSH, a score out of 100, and fixes that wait for Run.
  • Access management: see who can log in where, and remove a person's key from every server in one step.
  • Port forwarding: tunnels bound to 127.0.0.1, so databases can stay off the internet.

CtrlOps pricing

  • Free: $0, up to 2 servers on 2 devices.
  • Personal: $9 a month, $90 a year or $349 one-time (1 seat).
  • Team: $39 a month, $390 a year, or $849 one-time (5 seats).
  • Enterprise: $229 a month, $2,290 a year or $2,499 one-time (unlimited seats).

Docker management is $10 a month ($100 a year) extra on Personal, and included in every Lifetime plan and in Enterprise. Each paid seat works on up to 2 devices, and Personal has a 14-day free trial with no card. Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: managing many servers; Docker, one-click deploys, an AI terminal and monitoring in one app; and keeping passwords and keys on your own computer.

Limitations

  • No mobile app: CtrlOps is desktop-only, for macOS, Windows, and Linux.
  • No serverless support: CtrlOps manages Linux servers you reach over SSH, so serverless functions such as AWS Lambda or Google Cloud Functions are out of scope.
  • No Kubernetes or container orchestration: Docker management covers Docker Engine and Docker Compose on each server. CtrlOps does not manage Kubernetes or Swarm.

2. Termius: a cross-platform client with optional cloud sync

Termius is an SSH client for Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS and Android. Desktop version 10.4.1 came out on 9 November 2026.

Where your keys live: The free Starter plan keeps a local vault on one device. Paid plans add a cloud vault that syncs, end-to-end encrypted with a key derived from your password. The "Sync keys and identities" toggle keeps keys and passwords local. Connections go straight to your servers: "Termius is not a proxy" (security page).

Key features

  • SSH, SFTP and port forwarding: on the free Starter plan.
  • FIDO2 security keys: hardware keys such as YubiKey.
  • Biometric SSH keys: stored in Secure Enclave, TPM or Android Keystore; not synced.
  • 2FA: TOTP or Authy for email sign-in; team owners can require it.
  • Team vaults: shared hosts with "Can edit" or "Can view" rights (Team plan and up).

Termius pricing

  • Starter: free.
  • Pro: $10 a month, paid annually.
  • Team: $20 per seat a month, paid annually (minimum 2 seats).
  • Business: $30 per seat a month, paid annually.
  • Enterprise: custom pricing.

Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: phone access and shared team vaults.

Limitations

  • Your account is part of your security: with sync on, your encrypted vault also lives in the Termius cloud.
  • Logs on by default: paid plans record session logs in every vault, and turning logging off deletes them.
  • Starter can lose data: logging out or removing the app deletes changes that were never synced.

3. PuTTY: the free, minimal client for Windows

PuTTY is a free SSH and Telnet client for Windows, with no official Mac version. Version 0.85 came out on 16 August 2026.

Where your keys live: sessions and host keys sit in the Windows Registry (HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY). PuTTY does not remember passwords. Keys sit in .ppk files, and a key with no passphrase is "saved unencrypted".

Key features

  • Pageant: an SSH agent holding decrypted keys in memory.
  • Host key checks: warns on new or changed server keys; always on.
  • Port forwarding: local, remote and dynamic (SOCKS) tunnels.
  • File transfer: separate command-line tools PSCP and PSFTP.
  • Privacy: sends nothing to its developers; session logging is off by default.

PuTTY pricing

  • Free: the only edition.

Checked on 25 November 2026 in the official PuTTY FAQ.

Best for: quick, minimal connections on Windows.

Limitations

  • No tabs: tabs are a low-priority item on its official wishlist.
  • Terminal only: no server tools such as monitoring or deployments.
  • Keep it updated: 0.84 (May 2026) and 0.85 (August 2026) both fixed security issues.

4. MobaXterm: a Windows toolbox with SSH, SFTP and X11

MobaXterm is a Windows terminal with an X11 server, a tabbed SSH client and network tools. Version 26.6 came out on 25 October 2026.

Where your keys live: sessions and settings sit in MobaXterm.ini on your PC. Saved passwords sit behind a master password, on the free Home edition too. You pick a key file for each session.

Key features

  • SFTP browser: opens on SSH login, with drag-and-drop transfers.
  • Tabs and split view: 2 or 4 terminals side by side.
  • SSH tunnel manager: a graphical tool for creating tunnels.
  • Multi-execution: runs the same commands on many servers at once.
  • Terminal logs: output saved to local text files.

MobaXterm pricing

  • Home: free.
  • Professional: $69 per user, excluding tax, with 12 months of updates. You keep the version you bought.

Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official download page.

Best for: X11 and many tools on Windows.

Limitations

  • Windows only: no official Mac or Linux version.
  • Home limits: 12 sessions, 2 SSH tunnels, and 4 macros.
  • Company rollout needs Pro: one person may use Home at work, but deploying it across a company, or sharing one install, needs Professional.

5. SecureCRT: a paid, cross-platform client for admins who script

SecureCRT is VanDyke Software's terminal emulator with SSH support for Windows, macOS and Linux, plus a separate iOS app. Version 9.7.4 came out on 3 November 2026.

Where your keys live: on your computer, with sessions as .ini files in a local configuration folder. Saved passwords are encrypted in the configuration, and an optional configuration passphrase locks them. Key files sit in a local folder (named "Identity" by default) behind the key's passphrase.

SecureCRT's pages describe no cloud sync of its own: you move sessions with Export Settings and Import.

Key features

  • Automation: Python 3 scripts, custom button bar and Command Manager.
  • SFTP tab: on a connected SSH2 session; SecureFX is the separate file transfer app.
  • Smart cards: public-key logins with X.509 certificates; PKCS #11 tokens also work.
  • SSH agent: registered keys sign you in, even after SecureCRT closes.
  • FIPS mode: a FIPS 140-2 validated cryptographic library.

SecureCRT pricing (one licence)

  • SecureCRT with 1 year of updates: $119.
  • SecureCRT with 3 years of updates: $190.

SecureCRT is "licensed per computer, not per user or server", with a perpetual licence to the version you buy. Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: one paid client on Windows, macOS and Linux, with Python scripting.

Limitations

  • No free plan: after the 30-day evaluation, you buy a licence. Updates stop after the 1 or 3 years you paid for.
  • Platform limits: FIPS mode is Windows-only, and the Linux requirements list only Ubuntu and Kubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 LTS.
  • Keep it updated: its advisories cover Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795, fixed in 9.4.3) and OpenSSL issues (fixed in 9.5.1), with none listed for 2025 or 2026.

Which tools give you an SSH terminal in the browser?

Coolify, aaPanel, and Webmin each have a terminal page in the browser. If you run a VPS, you likely have one of these already.

6. Coolify: a self-hosted app platform with a web terminal

Coolify is an open-source, self-hostable platform for deploying apps, databases, and services. Version 4.7.6 came out on 19 November 2026, and v4 left beta in April 2026.

Where your keys live: on the Coolify server. Coolify encrypts the private-key value in its database. When self-hosted, it also writes the key as a file under /data/coolify/ssh/keys/, and its SSH Keys docs do not say those files are encrypted. Keys must not have a passphrase.

Key features

  • Web Terminal: team owners and admins only; sessions end after 8 hours.
  • 2FA: optional, with a TOTP app; owners and admins can require it for everyone.
  • Team roles: Owner, Admin and Member; Members are read-only by default.
  • Git deploys: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Gitea, with deploy on push.
  • Database backups: scheduled, copied to S3-compatible, SFTP, FTPS or WebDAV storage.

Coolify pricing

  • Self-hosted: free.
  • Coolify Cloud: $5 a month for 2 servers, plus $3 a month per extra server.

Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: quick shells for Coolify users.

Limitations

  • A high-value target: the dashboard holds your keys and opens shells.
  • Port 6002: it must be open for the terminal when you open the dashboard by IP on port 8000.
  • Root by default: the setup guide connects as root; a non-root user is experimental and needs passwordless sudo.

7. aaPanel: a hosting panel with a built-in terminal

aaPanel is a web hosting control panel installed on the server itself. Version 8.0.8 came out on 23 November 2026.

Where your keys live: The Terminal opens the local server by default, with no key. For another server, you enter its IP, port, SSH account, and a password or private key. aaPanel's docs do not say whether the Terminal saves that password or key.

Key features

  • Terminal: includes a list of saved commands.
  • Login protection: random security path, Google Authenticator, BasicAuth and IP allow list.
  • Server security: firewall rules, SSH login settings and brute force protection.
  • File manager: upload, download, unpack and edit files online.
  • Scheduled backups: sites, databases, and folders to local disk, FTP or cloud storage.

aaPanel pricing

  • Free: $0.
  • Pro, monthly: $28.80 a month.
  • Pro, yearly: $198 a year.
  • Pro, lifetime: $699 one-time.

Pro has a 14-day trial. Regular prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: PHP sites and databases on a VPS.

Limitations

  • Some commands break the Terminal: the docs say not to run bt restart, bt stop or bt 1 there; use an SSH tool.
  • A public login page: restrict the panel login, and keep the URL, port and random path that the installer prints private.
  • One licence per server: each Pro licence covers one server.

8. Webmin: a system admin panel with a Terminal module

Webmin is a web-based system administration tool for Unix-like servers. Version 2.670 came out in September 2026.

Where your keys live: Webmin asks for no SSH key. Its Terminal module opens a shell on the Webmin server, behind the Webmin login. Since 2.200, sudo-capable users get a shell as themselves instead of as root.

Key features

  • Terminal module: browser shell over WebSocket (Apache proxy guide).
  • Login security: 2FA with Google Authenticator or Authy, and IP access control.
  • Server security: FirewallD, iptables or nftables rules, Fail2Ban and SSH server settings.
  • Webmin users: extra logins limited to some modules and actions.
  • File Manager: browse, edit, upload and download files online.

Webmin pricing

  • Free: the only edition, also for commercial use.

Checked on 25 November 2026 on the official About page.

Best for: deep admin work on one server from a browser.

Limitations

  • Not safe to expose with the defaults: Webmin runs with full root privileges on port 10000. Its docs say "By default Webmin will accept connections from any IP address" and advise limiting access to legitimate client systems.
  • Keep it updated: 2.670 fixed a privilege-escalation issue in Custom Commands.

Where do your keys and session data live, and who can reach them?

With a desktop client, your keys live on your computer and only your computer talks to the server. With most web-based tools, the panel or gateway stores your key or password, or opens the shell itself. Anyone who gets into that layer can reach your server without your key.

Risk Desktop client Web-based tool What to check
Where the private key is stored On your computer (apps that sync, such as Termius paid plans, also keep an encrypted cloud copy) On the panel or gateway server (Coolify: in its database and key files) The tool's docs on storage and encryption
A breach of the panel or gateway No panel to breach; your laptop is the target Whoever gets in can use stored keys or open a shell Its advisories and how fast fixes ship
A public login page or port Nothing new; only the SSH port The panel login is reachable (Webmin: port 10000, any IP by default) IP allow list, VPN, 2FA
Browser extensions and page scripts Not in a browser An extension with access to all sites can read the page; page scripts can read local storage Your installed extensions
Who sees your session in plain text Only your computer and the server The panel or gateway that opens the shell Where SSH encryption ends
When the service is down No panel in the path You lose that path (normal SSH still works if its port is open) A second way in
Team access and session records Per person; Termius Team and Business add shared vaults and logs, and SecureCRT can log to a file One shared login page with team roles (Coolify: only owners and admins can use the terminal, and 2FA can be required) Whether you need recorded sessions

Sources for the browser row: Chrome Web Store Help and the OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet.

Is a web-based SSH client safe?

A web-based SSH client can be safe when you host the panel or gateway yourself, patch it and keep its login off the open internet. The risk is not the browser. It is the layer in the middle, which stores your keys or can open a shell.

"Coolify stores SSH private keys and uses them to run commands on connected servers."

  • Coolify documentation, Security Model

In July 2026, Coolify published two Critical advisories (CVSS 9.9) about its terminal WebSocket. A low-privileged team member could run commands on team servers (CVE-2026-34048) or get the host SSH private key (CVE-2026-34047). Both are fixed in 4.0.0-beta.471.

If you keep a web path, lock it down:

  • Put a VPN or an IP allow list in front of the panel.
  • Turn on 2FA. All three panels support it.
  • Install updates as soon as they ship.
  • Turn the terminal off where you do not need it (Coolify allows this per server).

For shell access, a desktop app over plain SSH, such as CtrlOps, adds no panel, login page or stored private key on the server.

What risks does a desktop SSH client still have?

A desktop client moves the risk to your own computer:

  • A stolen or infected laptop exposes whatever is saved on it.
  • A key with no passphrase is not encrypted on disk.
  • Agent forwarding to a server you do not trust: the OpenSSH manual says "Agent forwarding should be enabled with caution." PuTTY 0.85 fixed a Pageant issue reachable that way.

What helps:

  • A passphrase on every key, or a hardware-backed key (OpenSSH -sk keys, since 8.2).
  • A passphrase on the app's saved data: CtrlOps Vault Lock, the MobaXterm master password or the SecureCRT configuration passphrase.
  • Client updates.

Which should you use for production servers?

Use a desktop client as your daily path to production, and keep one locked-down web path as a backup.

  • Solo developer or small team on a few VPS: a desktop client. Plain ssh is enough if you only need a shell.
  • Keys on your computer, plus server tools (files, monitoring, deploys, Docker, a security audit) with no web panel or agent: CtrlOps.
  • The same hosts on your phone, or one shared team vault: Termius (sync and shared vaults are on paid plans).
  • Windows, free and minimal: PuTTY.
  • Windows with X11 and many tools: MobaXterm.
  • Python scripting with a perpetual licence per computer, or FIPS 140-2 mode on Windows: SecureCRT.
  • You already deploy with Coolify: use its terminal for quick checks, with 2FA on and the terminal off where it is not needed.
  • PHP sites or deep system admin from a panel: keep aaPanel or Webmin, with the login locked down.

Desktop first is not for everyone. Teams whose rules require every session to pass one central gateway that records it need that gateway. So do people who cannot install apps on the computer they work from.

Before you pick any tool, ask one question: where does my key live, and who else can reach it? And which do you use for production today: a desktop client, a panel terminal, or both?

I wrote more about keeping my own workflow local in Building a Local-First DevOps Workflow Without Cloud Sync.

If you want to try the desktop route with server tools included, CtrlOps has a free plan for 2 servers.

I'm Hiren Kalariya, co-founder of CtrlOps. I write about SSH, Linux servers and local-first DevOps tools.

FAQ

Do aaPanel, Coolify and Webmin store my SSH keys?

Coolify does: it encrypts private keys in its database and, when self-hosted, also writes key files on the server. aaPanel's docs do not say whether its Terminal saves passwords or keys for other servers. Webmin's Terminal asks for no key.

Which SSH client makes it easy to manage dozens of servers?

A desktop client with a saved server list. CtrlOps keeps every server in one list, each in its own tab, with no agent on the servers (unlimited on paid plans, 2 on Free). Termius syncs hosts across devices on paid plans.

Do I need a control panel on every server?

No. aaPanel and Webmin run on the server they manage. A desktop app such as CtrlOps manages each server over SSH from your computer, with no panel on any of them.

Which SSH tools record or log sessions?

Termius keeps session logs on paid plans, on by default. SecureCRT can start logging to a file when it connects, with a timestamp on each line. MobaXterm and PuTTY can write terminal output to a local file.

Is Termius safe for production servers?

Termius connects straight to your servers and encrypts synced data end to end. To keep keys local, use the free plan or turn off "Sync keys and identities".

Is PuTTY or MobaXterm safe?

Both run locally and are safe when kept updated: PuTTY 0.84 and 0.85 (2026) and recent MobaXterm releases fixed security issues.

Which SSH client is the most secure?

The ssh command from OpenSSH is the reference most clients are compared with. Still, no client makes a weak key or an open server safe: most of your security comes from the key and the server's settings. If your rules require FIPS 140-2, SecureCRT has a FIPS mode on Windows.

event_model_payload.headline: Web-Based vs Desktop SSH Clients: 8 Tools and Which Is Safer
event_model_payload.summary:
For production servers, a desktop SSH client is the safer default. Your private key stays on your computer, and nothing new listens on the server.

Most web-based tools put a gateway or panel between your browser and the server, and that layer holds your keys or can open a shell. Keep one web path as a locked-down backup.

TL;DR

  • Desktop clients (CtrlOps, Termius, PuTTY, MobaXterm, SecureCRT) connect straight to the server. Your key stays on your device (Termius can also sync an encrypted copy).
  • Web-based tools (a web SSH gateway, or a panel like Coolify, aaPanel or Webmin) open the shell for you, and Coolify stores your private keys.
  • If you also want server tools with no web panel, server agent or cloud sync, CtrlOps does this in one desktop app. It covers files, monitoring, deploys, Docker and a security audit.

I made a short video on the same question:

What is a desktop SSH client and how does it work?

A desktop SSH client is an app on your computer that opens the SSH connection straight to the server. The private key stays on your disk, in your OS keychain or on a hardware key. The server needs only its normal SSH service.

your computer (app + key) --SSH--> your server

The simplest desktop client is the ssh command from OpenSSH (10.6, October 2026). It works in the macOS Terminal and installs as a package on Linux. On Windows 10 (build 1809 and later) and Windows 11, it is available as an optional feature. Keys live in ~/.ssh/ by default.

GUI clients such as CtrlOps, Termius, PuTTY, MobaXterm and SecureCRT work the same way and add saved sessions and other tools.

The trade-off: you install the app on each computer, and each person connects with their own keys, so a team gets no single login page.

What is a web-based SSH client and how does it work?

A web-based SSH client gives you a terminal in a browser tab, so yes, you can SSH from a browser. A browser cannot open raw SSH connections, so a server in the middle talks HTTPS or WebSocket to the browser and SSH to the server.

browser --HTTPS/WebSocket--> gateway or panel --SSH--> your server

There are three kinds:

  • A web SSH gateway: a web app, hosted by you, a vendor or a cloud provider, opens the SSH connection and shows the terminal.
  • A server panel with a terminal page: Coolify, aaPanel and Webmin open a shell after you log in. Strictly, they are panels, not SSH clients.
  • An in-browser client: the SSH client runs inside the page, as in ssheasy. Its site says no credentials are shared with its servers, which only tunnel the packets.

For a longer comparison, see these 7 key differences between web-based and local SSH clients.

How do the 8 tools compare?

Desktop apps keep keys on your computer by default; web panels run on your server:

Tool Type Where your keys or logins live Installed on your server? Synced to a vendor cloud? Free option
CtrlOps Desktop app (Mac, Windows, Linux) On your computer: saved servers and passwords AES-256 encrypted; a key file you pick stays where it is No agent No, on any plan Yes, 2 servers
Termius Desktop and mobile app On your device; paid plans also sync an end-to-end encrypted vault No Paid plans (keys can stay local) Yes, Starter
PuTTY Desktop app (Windows) Sessions in the Windows Registry; keys in .ppk files; no saved passwords No No Yes, free
MobaXterm Desktop app (Windows) Sessions in MobaXterm.ini; saved passwords behind a master password No No Yes, Home (12 sessions)
SecureCRT Desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux), plus iOS On your computer: local config files, encrypted saved passwords, optional configuration passphrase, local key files No None described; you export and import sessions No, 30-day trial
Coolify Self-hosted app platform with a web terminal On the Coolify server: encrypted in its database, plus key files Yes No, when self-hosted Yes, self-hosted
aaPanel Hosting panel with a terminal No key for its own server; for other servers, its docs do not say if it saves your password or key Yes Not stated Yes, free edition
Webmin System admin panel with a terminal No SSH key: the Webmin login opens a shell on its own server Yes No Yes, free

Which desktop SSH clients keep your keys on your computer?

CtrlOps, Termius, PuTTY, MobaXterm and SecureCRT all keep your private keys on your computer by default. CtrlOps has no cloud sync on any plan, and Termius syncs an encrypted vault only on paid plans.

1. CtrlOps: a local-first desktop app for server management

CtrlOps is a local-first desktop app for AI-assisted Linux server management.

It runs on Mac (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows (Microsoft Store), and Linux (Ubuntu 22.04+ and Debian 12+). Version 2.0.0 came out on 14 November 2026. It needs no agent on your servers.

"The fact that I don't need to install any agent on my servers sold me immediately."

  • Srushti Vasani, Product Hunt review

Where your keys live: on your computer, never on a CtrlOps server. Saved servers and remembered passwords are AES-256 encrypted on disk. The key that unlocks them sits in your OS keychain when available, with a copy in the app's storage. A key file you pick stays where it is (for example, ~/.ssh/), and CtrlOps saves only its path.

Optional Vault Lock asks for a passphrase at every start. Your servers and keys never sync to a cloud, and the privacy policy says your credentials, SSH keys, commands and logs never reach CtrlOps. Details: where CtrlOps stores your SSH keys and what it encrypts.

Key features

  • AI terminal: each terminal command the AI writes waits until you click Run.
  • File manager: uploads, downloads and edits over your SSH connection.
  • Live monitoring: no agent, refreshed every 2 seconds.
  • One-click deployment: Node.js, React, Next.js and static builds from GitHub.
  • Docker management: containers and Compose over SSH, with no Docker socket on the internet.
  • Security audit: 25 read-only audits over SSH, a score out of 100, and fixes that wait for Run.
  • Access management: see who can log in where, and remove a person's key from every server in one step.
  • Port forwarding: tunnels bound to 127.0.0.1, so databases can stay off the internet.

CtrlOps pricing

  • Free: $0, up to 2 servers on 2 devices.
  • Personal: $9 a month, $90 a year or $349 one-time (1 seat).
  • Team: $39 a month, $390 a year, or $849 one-time (5 seats).
  • Enterprise: $229 a month, $2,290 a year or $2,499 one-time (unlimited seats).

Docker management is $10 a month ($100 a year) extra on Personal, and included in every Lifetime plan and in Enterprise. Each paid seat works on up to 2 devices, and Personal has a 14-day free trial with no card. Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: managing many servers; Docker, one-click deploys, an AI terminal and monitoring in one app; and keeping passwords and keys on your own computer.

Limitations

  • No mobile app: CtrlOps is desktop-only, for macOS, Windows, and Linux.
  • No serverless support: CtrlOps manages Linux servers you reach over SSH, so serverless functions such as AWS Lambda or Google Cloud Functions are out of scope.
  • No Kubernetes or container orchestration: Docker management covers Docker Engine and Docker Compose on each server. CtrlOps does not manage Kubernetes or Swarm.

2. Termius: a cross-platform client with optional cloud sync

Termius is an SSH client for Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS and Android. Desktop version 10.4.1 came out on 9 November 2026.

Where your keys live: The free Starter plan keeps a local vault on one device. Paid plans add a cloud vault that syncs, end-to-end encrypted with a key derived from your password. The "Sync keys and identities" toggle keeps keys and passwords local. Connections go straight to your servers: "Termius is not a proxy" (security page).

Key features

  • SSH, SFTP and port forwarding: on the free Starter plan.
  • FIDO2 security keys: hardware keys such as YubiKey.
  • Biometric SSH keys: stored in Secure Enclave, TPM or Android Keystore; not synced.
  • 2FA: TOTP or Authy for email sign-in; team owners can require it.
  • Team vaults: shared hosts with "Can edit" or "Can view" rights (Team plan and up).

Termius pricing

  • Starter: free.
  • Pro: $10 a month, paid annually.
  • Team: $20 per seat a month, paid annually (minimum 2 seats).
  • Business: $30 per seat a month, paid annually.
  • Enterprise: custom pricing.

Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: phone access and shared team vaults.

Limitations

  • Your account is part of your security: with sync on, your encrypted vault also lives in the Termius cloud.
  • Logs on by default: paid plans record session logs in every vault, and turning logging off deletes them.
  • Starter can lose data: logging out or removing the app deletes changes that were never synced.

3. PuTTY: the free, minimal client for Windows

PuTTY is a free SSH and Telnet client for Windows, with no official Mac version. Version 0.85 came out on 16 August 2026.

Where your keys live: sessions and host keys sit in the Windows Registry (HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY). PuTTY does not remember passwords. Keys sit in .ppk files, and a key with no passphrase is "saved unencrypted".

Key features

  • Pageant: an SSH agent holding decrypted keys in memory.
  • Host key checks: warns on new or changed server keys; always on.
  • Port forwarding: local, remote and dynamic (SOCKS) tunnels.
  • File transfer: separate command-line tools PSCP and PSFTP.
  • Privacy: sends nothing to its developers; session logging is off by default.

PuTTY pricing

  • Free: the only edition.

Checked on 25 November 2026 in the official PuTTY FAQ.

Best for: quick, minimal connections on Windows.

Limitations

  • No tabs: tabs are a low-priority item on its official wishlist.
  • Terminal only: no server tools such as monitoring or deployments.
  • Keep it updated: 0.84 (May 2026) and 0.85 (August 2026) both fixed security issues.

4. MobaXterm: a Windows toolbox with SSH, SFTP and X11

MobaXterm is a Windows terminal with an X11 server, a tabbed SSH client and network tools. Version 26.6 came out on 25 October 2026.

Where your keys live: sessions and settings sit in MobaXterm.ini on your PC. Saved passwords sit behind a master password, on the free Home edition too. You pick a key file for each session.

Key features

  • SFTP browser: opens on SSH login, with drag-and-drop transfers.
  • Tabs and split view: 2 or 4 terminals side by side.
  • SSH tunnel manager: a graphical tool for creating tunnels.
  • Multi-execution: runs the same commands on many servers at once.
  • Terminal logs: output saved to local text files.

MobaXterm pricing

  • Home: free.
  • Professional: $69 per user, excluding tax, with 12 months of updates. You keep the version you bought.

Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official download page.

Best for: X11 and many tools on Windows.

Limitations

  • Windows only: no official Mac or Linux version.
  • Home limits: 12 sessions, 2 SSH tunnels, and 4 macros.
  • Company rollout needs Pro: one person may use Home at work, but deploying it across a company, or sharing one install, needs Professional.

5. SecureCRT: a paid, cross-platform client for admins who script

SecureCRT is VanDyke Software's terminal emulator with SSH support for Windows, macOS and Linux, plus a separate iOS app. Version 9.7.4 came out on 3 November 2026.

Where your keys live: on your computer, with sessions as .ini files in a local configuration folder. Saved passwords are encrypted in the configuration, and an optional configuration passphrase locks them. Key files sit in a local folder (named "Identity" by default) behind the key's passphrase.

SecureCRT's pages describe no cloud sync of its own: you move sessions with Export Settings and Import.

Key features

  • Automation: Python 3 scripts, custom button bar and Command Manager.
  • SFTP tab: on a connected SSH2 session; SecureFX is the separate file transfer app.
  • Smart cards: public-key logins with X.509 certificates; PKCS #11 tokens also work.
  • SSH agent: registered keys sign you in, even after SecureCRT closes.
  • FIPS mode: a FIPS 140-2 validated cryptographic library.

SecureCRT pricing (one licence)

  • SecureCRT with 1 year of updates: $119.
  • SecureCRT with 3 years of updates: $190.

SecureCRT is "licensed per computer, not per user or server", with a perpetual licence to the version you buy. Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: one paid client on Windows, macOS and Linux, with Python scripting.

Limitations

  • No free plan: after the 30-day evaluation, you buy a licence. Updates stop after the 1 or 3 years you paid for.
  • Platform limits: FIPS mode is Windows-only, and the Linux requirements list only Ubuntu and Kubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 LTS.
  • Keep it updated: its advisories cover Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795, fixed in 9.4.3) and OpenSSL issues (fixed in 9.5.1), with none listed for 2025 or 2026.

Which tools give you an SSH terminal in the browser?

Coolify, aaPanel, and Webmin each have a terminal page in the browser. If you run a VPS, you likely have one of these already.

6. Coolify: a self-hosted app platform with a web terminal

Coolify is an open-source, self-hostable platform for deploying apps, databases, and services. Version 4.7.6 came out on 19 November 2026, and v4 left beta in April 2026.

Where your keys live: on the Coolify server. Coolify encrypts the private-key value in its database. When self-hosted, it also writes the key as a file under /data/coolify/ssh/keys/, and its SSH Keys docs do not say those files are encrypted. Keys must not have a passphrase.

Key features

  • Web Terminal: team owners and admins only; sessions end after 8 hours.
  • 2FA: optional, with a TOTP app; owners and admins can require it for everyone.
  • Team roles: Owner, Admin and Member; Members are read-only by default.
  • Git deploys: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Gitea, with deploy on push.
  • Database backups: scheduled, copied to S3-compatible, SFTP, FTPS or WebDAV storage.

Coolify pricing

  • Self-hosted: free.
  • Coolify Cloud: $5 a month for 2 servers, plus $3 a month per extra server.

Prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: quick shells for Coolify users.

Limitations

  • A high-value target: the dashboard holds your keys and opens shells.
  • Port 6002: it must be open for the terminal when you open the dashboard by IP on port 8000.
  • Root by default: the setup guide connects as root; a non-root user is experimental and needs passwordless sudo.

7. aaPanel: a hosting panel with a built-in terminal

aaPanel is a web hosting control panel installed on the server itself. Version 8.0.8 came out on 23 November 2026.

Where your keys live: The Terminal opens the local server by default, with no key. For another server, you enter its IP, port, SSH account, and a password or private key. aaPanel's docs do not say whether the Terminal saves that password or key.

Key features

  • Terminal: includes a list of saved commands.
  • Login protection: random security path, Google Authenticator, BasicAuth and IP allow list.
  • Server security: firewall rules, SSH login settings and brute force protection.
  • File manager: upload, download, unpack and edit files online.
  • Scheduled backups: sites, databases, and folders to local disk, FTP or cloud storage.

aaPanel pricing

  • Free: $0.
  • Pro, monthly: $28.80 a month.
  • Pro, yearly: $198 a year.
  • Pro, lifetime: $699 one-time.

Pro has a 14-day trial. Regular prices checked on 25 November 2026 on the official pricing page.

Best for: PHP sites and databases on a VPS.

Limitations

  • Some commands break the Terminal: the docs say not to run bt restart, bt stop or bt 1 there; use an SSH tool.
  • A public login page: restrict the panel login, and keep the URL, port and random path that the installer prints private.
  • One licence per server: each Pro licence covers one server.

8. Webmin: a system admin panel with a Terminal module

Webmin is a web-based system administration tool for Unix-like servers. Version 2.670 came out in September 2026.

Where your keys live: Webmin asks for no SSH key. Its Terminal module opens a shell on the Webmin server, behind the Webmin login. Since 2.200, sudo-capable users get a shell as themselves instead of as root.

Key features

  • Terminal module: browser shell over WebSocket (Apache proxy guide).
  • Login security: 2FA with Google Authenticator or Authy, and IP access control.
  • Server security: FirewallD, iptables or nftables rules, Fail2Ban and SSH server settings.
  • Webmin users: extra logins limited to some modules and actions.
  • File Manager: browse, edit, upload and download files online.

Webmin pricing

  • Free: the only edition, also for commercial use.

Checked on 25 November 2026 on the official About page.

Best for: deep admin work on one server from a browser.

Limitations

  • Not safe to expose with the defaults: Webmin runs with full root privileges on port 10000. Its docs say "By default Webmin will accept connections from any IP address" and advise limiting access to legitimate client systems.
  • Keep it updated: 2.670 fixed a privilege-escalation issue in Custom Commands.

Where do your keys and session data live, and who can reach them?

With a desktop client, your keys live on your computer and only your computer talks to the server. With most web-based tools, the panel or gateway stores your key or password, or opens the shell itself. Anyone who gets into that layer can reach your server without your key.

Risk Desktop client Web-based tool What to check
Where the private key is stored On your computer (apps that sync, such as Termius paid plans, also keep an encrypted cloud copy) On the panel or gateway server (Coolify: in its database and key files) The tool's docs on storage and encryption
A breach of the panel or gateway No panel to breach; your laptop is the target Whoever gets in can use stored keys or open a shell Its advisories and how fast fixes ship
A public login page or port Nothing new; only the SSH port The panel login is reachable (Webmin: port 10000, any IP by default) IP allow list, VPN, 2FA
Browser extensions and page scripts Not in a browser An extension with access to all sites can read the page; page scripts can read local storage Your installed extensions
Who sees your session in plain text Only your computer and the server The panel or gateway that opens the shell Where SSH encryption ends
When the service is down No panel in the path You lose that path (normal SSH still works if its port is open) A second way in
Team access and session records Per person; Termius Team and Business add shared vaults and logs, and SecureCRT can log to a file One shared login page with team roles (Coolify: only owners and admins can use the terminal, and 2FA can be required) Whether you need recorded sessions

Sources for the browser row: Chrome Web Store Help and the OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet.

Is a web-based SSH client safe?

A web-based SSH client can be safe when you host the panel or gateway yourself, patch it and keep its login off the open internet. The risk is not the browser. It is the layer in the middle, which stores your keys or can open a shell.

"Coolify stores SSH private keys and uses them to run commands on connected servers."

  • Coolify documentation, Security Model

In July 2026, Coolify published two Critical advisories (CVSS 9.9) about its terminal WebSocket. A low-privileged team member could run commands on team servers (CVE-2026-34048) or get the host SSH private key (CVE-2026-34047). Both are fixed in 4.0.0-beta.471.

If you keep a web path, lock it down:

  • Put a VPN or an IP allow list in front of the panel.
  • Turn on 2FA. All three panels support it.
  • Install updates as soon as they ship.
  • Turn the terminal off where you do not need it (Coolify allows this per server).

For shell access, a desktop app over plain SSH, such as CtrlOps, adds no panel, login page or stored private key on the server.

What risks does a desktop SSH client still have?

A desktop client moves the risk to your own computer:

  • A stolen or infected laptop exposes whatever is saved on it.
  • A key with no passphrase is not encrypted on disk.
  • Agent forwarding to a server you do not trust: the OpenSSH manual says "Agent forwarding should be enabled with caution." PuTTY 0.85 fixed a Pageant issue reachable that way.

What helps:

  • A passphrase on every key, or a hardware-backed key (OpenSSH -sk keys, since 8.2).
  • A passphrase on the app's saved data: CtrlOps Vault Lock, the MobaXterm master password or the SecureCRT configuration passphrase.
  • Client updates.

Which should you use for production servers?

Use a desktop client as your daily path to production, and keep one locked-down web path as a backup.

  • Solo developer or small team on a few VPS: a desktop client. Plain ssh is enough if you only need a shell.
  • Keys on your computer, plus server tools (files, monitoring, deploys, Docker, a security audit) with no web panel or agent: CtrlOps.
  • The same hosts on your phone, or one shared team vault: Termius (sync and shared vaults are on paid plans).
  • Windows, free and minimal: PuTTY.
  • Windows with X11 and many tools: MobaXterm.
  • Python scripting with a perpetual licence per computer, or FIPS 140-2 mode on Windows: SecureCRT.
  • You already deploy with Coolify: use its terminal for quick checks, with 2FA on and the terminal off where it is not needed.
  • PHP sites or deep system admin from a panel: keep aaPanel or Webmin, with the login locked down.

Desktop first is not for everyone. Teams whose rules require every session to pass one central gateway that records it need that gateway. So do people who cannot install apps on the computer they work from.

Before you pick any tool, ask one question: where does my key live, and who else can reach it? And which do you use for production today: a desktop client, a panel terminal, or both?

I wrote more about keeping my own workflow local in Building a Local-First DevOps Workflow Without Cloud Sync.

If you want to try the desktop route with server tools included, CtrlOps has a free plan for 2 servers.

I'm Hiren Kalariya, co-founder of CtrlOps. I write about SSH, Linux servers and local-first DevOps tools.

FAQ

Do aaPanel, Coolify and Webmin store my SSH keys?

Coolify does: it encrypts private keys in its database and, when self-hosted, also writes key files on the server. aaPanel's docs do not say whether its Terminal saves passwords or keys for other servers. Webmin's Terminal asks for no key.

Which SSH client makes it easy to manage dozens of servers?

A desktop client with a saved server list. CtrlOps keeps every server in one list, each in its own tab, with no agent on the servers (unlimited on paid plans, 2 on Free). Termius syncs hosts across devices on paid plans.

Do I need a control panel on every server?

No. aaPanel and Webmin run on the server they manage. A desktop app such as CtrlOps manages each server over SSH from your computer, with no panel on any of them.

Which SSH tools record or log sessions?

Termius keeps session logs on paid plans, on by default. SecureCRT can start logging to a file when it connects, with a timestamp on each line. MobaXterm and PuTTY can write terminal output to a local file.

Is Termius safe for production servers?

Termius connects straight to your servers and encrypts synced data end to end. To keep keys local, use the free plan or turn off "Sync keys and identities".

Is PuTTY or MobaXterm safe?

Both run locally and are safe when kept updated: PuTTY 0.84 and 0.85 (2026) and recent MobaXterm releases fixed security issues.

Which SSH client is the most secure?

The ssh command from OpenSSH is the reference most clients are compared with. Still, no client makes a weak key or an open server safe: most of your security comes from the key and the server's settings. If your rules require FIPS 140-2, SecureCRT has a FIPS mode on Windows.

title: Making agent retries safe across timeouts and restarts
summary:
Imagine an enterprise support agent ordering an approved replacement for a customer. The order goes through, but the confirmation times out. The agent retries and reports success. Two orders are now queued for fulfillment, and the support team has a duplicate to sort out.

That sequence is easy to miss if the only thing you check is whether the retry succeeded. To reproduce it, this experiment uses a small HTTP order service and a scripted tool caller. In the first timeout case, the caller gave up after about 101 ms. The order had already been committed. Retrying created another row with the same tenant, product and quantity. The caller saw one timeout followed by a successful 201 Created.

The failure sits between the tool and the service, so reproducing it does not require a model. The setup uses two SQLite databases, one for the caller's saved state and one for the service's orders. All failures are injected locally. This is a deployment exercise, not a report from a customer environment.

Across three rounds, the experiment recorded 117 scenario runs and 288 HTTP requests, keeping failed attempts alongside successful ones. Reusing a saved operation key prevented duplicates in several cases. It was not enough when the service had no record of the earlier request, whether because that record was never saved or had already been deleted.

What happens between a tool call and its result

For the replacement order in the opening example, the tool request could be as small as this:

POST /orders
Content-Type: application/json

{"sku":"keyboard","quantity":1}

The service can commit this order and lose the connection before the response reaches the caller. To make that timing reproducible, the test gives the caller a 100 ms socket timeout and makes the service hold its response for 500 ms after committing. Here is the caller's record, with unrelated fields omitted:

{
  "fault": "timeout_after_commit",
  "timeout_seconds": 0.1,
  "status": null,
  "error_type": "TimeoutError",
  "error": "timed out",
  "elapsed_ms": 100.892311
}

The exception tells us how long the caller waited. To find out whether the order exists, we have to look at the server trace and database. Raising the timeout above 500 ms would let this particular response arrive, but it would leave the connection-drop and process-crash cases unresolved.

That is why increasing timeouts or adding backoff cannot settle the duplicate-order problem on its own. As AWS explains in its guidance on timeouts and retries, a failed call can still have side effects. Once the order is committed, a retry needs a way to identify it as work already done.

Three retry strategies, the same faults

An idempotency key gives the service an identifier it can recognize when the caller retries. To check what that actually protects, the experiment runs each scenario with three ways of identifying the request:

Strategy What the caller sends
No key The same payload again, without an operation identifier
New key per attempt A new UUID for every HTTP request
Durable action key One UUID saved for the intended action before the first request, then reused

The service supports keys throughout. What changes is the caller: it either omits the key, replaces it on every attempt, or saves and reuses it. A fresh UUID on each request still makes every retry look like new work, even though the payload has not changed.

The results below count orders created in one scenario run. Counting successful responses would miss the original problem. All three repetitions produced these counts.

Injected condition No key New key per attempt Durable action key
Response arrives normally 1 1 1
Caller times out after commit 2 2 1
Connection closes after commit 2 2 1
Service exits before commit, then restarts 1 1 1
Service exits after commit, then restarts 2 2 1
Caller process dies before its completion checkpoint 2 2 1
Eight concurrent deliveries of one intended action 8 8 1
All three responses are dropped 3 3 1

Notice the difference between a service exit before and after commit. Before commit, there is no saved order, so the next attempt should create one. After commit, creating another would be a duplicate. The service needs to return the result of the original order instead.

These counts describe deliberately injected faults, not their frequency in production traffic. They establish which behavior each strategy produces. To understand why the durable key works here, we need to follow where it is stored and how the service uses it.

Keep the identity outside the model conversation

For the support workflow, the key belongs to the approved replacement order. Retrying its HTTP request does not mean the customer approved another order.

The caller therefore saves a mapping from (tenant, action) to a random UUID before making the first request. A fresh invocation looks up the same action and gets the same key. Storing that mapping in SQLite lets it survive a caller restart; keeping it in a Python variable would not.

This only works if the workflow preserves the action identifier as well. After a restart, the test resumes action-1 and retrieves its saved key. Generating a new action ID at that point would lose the protection before the next HTTP request was sent. The same applies to model-driven tool calls: an SDK retry, a workflow retry and a resumed invocation may all be attempts to complete one approved action. Their identity needs to come from saved workflow state.

Two genuinely separate orders can have identical payloads. If a customer intentionally orders two keyboards in two transactions, hashing the payload as the operation key would incorrectly collapse the second order into the first. The distinct-action control sends the same payload with two action identities and correctly creates two orders.

A payload hash is still useful, but for a different check: whether a caller has changed the request while reusing an existing key. That check belongs on the service side.

The service has to make a promise it can keep

Recognizing the key is only half the job. The service also needs to know what happened when it first received that key. It stores a replay receipt: a record of the key, request fingerprint, response status and response body. When the same key and payload arrive again, the service returns that saved response, including the original order ID.

The order and its receipt are written together:

BEGIN IMMEDIATE
  look up (tenant, operation, key)
  if a receipt exists:
    reject a different payload, or return the saved response
  otherwise:
    insert the order
    insert its replay receipt
COMMIT

Both inserts occur in one transaction. If storing the receipt fails, the order insert rolls back too. One regression test forces exactly that failure with a SQLite trigger, then verifies that a later valid request can still create the order.

For concurrent deliveries, this example acquires the write transaction before reading the receipt. SQLite allows only one writer at a time. That makes the eight-request result straightforward: one request creates the order, and the other seven replay its result.

This choice also serializes unrelated writes. It is convenient for a small reproduction, but the test says nothing about its throughput at customer scale. A different database needs its own tested locking and conflict-handling path.

There are also boundaries the service must enforce when looking up a receipt. The key is scoped to the tenant and operation, so the same UUID in another tenant must not return the first tenant's order. title: Get new CVE alerts for the software you run using the free NVD API
summary:
If you run software, new CVEs are your problem the day they are published. Paid scanners are the full answer, but small teams can get most of the value from the free NVD (National Vulnerability Database) API. This post shows how to pull new serious CVEs for the products you run, and a real result from this week.

Disclosure: I built an Apify Actor on top of this API and it is paid per result. The NVD API itself is free and official.

Query the NVD API 

curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=nginx&cvssV3Severity=HIGH&pubStartDate=2026-11-11T00:00:00.000&pubEndDate=2026-11-25T00:00:00.000"

Useful parameters: keywordSearch, cvssV3Severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL), and a publish date window (max 120 days per request). Without an API key you are limited to about 5 requests per 30 seconds, so sleep between calls. A free key raises that.

Real result: HIGH severity CVEs published 11 to 25 Nov 2026

Keyword HIGH CVEs in window Example
nginx 1 CVE-2026-136412, OpenResty stream-lua-nginx-module use-after-free, CVSS 8.1
openssl 0 none
wordpress 7 CVE-2026-116758, a plugin stored XSS, CVSS 7.2 (plugins, not WordPress core)

Two lessons. First, keyword search is loose: a plugin "for WordPress" matches the keyword but does not mean WordPress core is affected. Second, NVD scores new CVEs with a delay, so a brand-new CVE can be unscored for days and will not show up under a severity filter.

Make it useful: only show what is new

The annoying part of any CVE feed is repeats. You want each run to return only CVEs you have not seen, above your severity bar, with context: is it on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and what is the CISA due date.

Automate it

My Actor, CVE Watch, takes a product list, remembers what it already showed you, and returns new CVEs with product, cve_id, severity, CVSS score and vector, a direct-match flag, the CISA known-exploited flag and due date, and a link. A webhook URL can send results to Slack. Strict matching keeps only CVEs where the product is in the affected list or the first 300 characters of the description.

Price: $2 per 1,000 CVEs returned, and since only new items return, most daily runs cost cents.

https://apify.com/lightdata-tools/cve-watch

title: WordPress Otomatik Günlük Bulut Yedekleme Stratejileri
summary:
WordPress Otomatik Günlük Bulut Yedekleme Stratejileri konusunda kurumsal bir WordPress web sitesine sahipseniz, yaşanan teknik aksaklıklar doğrudan müşteri kaybına, Google arama sıralamalarının gerilemesine ve şirketinizin dijital prestijinin zedelenmesine yol açabilir. Bu rehberimizde hatanın kök nedenlerini, sunucu ve kod seviyesindeki kesin çözüm adımlarını detaylı olarak inceliyoruz.

Uzman Notu:

Web sitenizde herhangi bir yapılandırma, kod veya veritabanı müdahalesi yapmadan önce mutlaka sunucunuzdan tam zaman damgalı bir veritabanı ve dosya yedeği (backup) alınız.

Sorunun Olası Kök Nedenleri

WordPress altyapısında Otomatik Günlük Bulut Yedekleme Stratejileri durumunun tetiklenmesine yol açan en yaygın 4 temel etken şunlardır:

  • Sunucu Kaynak ve Bellek Yetersizliği: PHP hafıza sınırının (memory_limit) veya işlem zaman aşımının (max_execution_time) aşılması.
  • Eklenti ve Tema Çakışmaları: Yeni güncellenen bir yazılımın mevcut çekirdek WordPress dosyaları veya diğer eklentilerle uyumsuzluk yaşaması.
  • Bozuk Yapılandırma Dosyaları: .htaccess, wp-config.php veya sunucu Nginx/Apache konfigürasyonundaki hatalı direktifler.
  • Veritabanı İndeks ve Bağlantı Hataları: MySQL servisinin aşırı yük altında kilitlenmesi veya tabloların çökmesi.

1. Adım: Hata Ayıklama (Debug) Modu ile Sorunun Kaynağını Belirleyin

Karanlıkta çözüm aramak yerine sorunun hangi eklentiden veya kod satırından kaynaklandığını nokta atışı tespit etmek gerekir. Bunun için web sitenizin ana dizininde yer alan wp-config.php dosyasını açarak aşağıdaki satırları ekleyin:

// Hata ayıklama modunu sessiz günlük kaydıyla açın
define( 'WP_DEBUG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_LOG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY', false );
@ini_set( 'display_errors', 0 );

Bu ayar ziyaretçilerinize herhangi bir hata kodu göstermez; ancak sunucunuzun arka planında /wp-content/debug.log dosyasını oluşturarak çöken fonksiyonu satır numarasıyla birlikte kaydeder.

2. Adım: Sunucu ve PHP Parametrelerini Optimize Edin

Kurumsal altyapılarda modern WordPress eklentileri (WooCommerce, Elementor, WPML vb.) yüksek bellek ve yürütme süresi talep eder. Hosting kontrol panelinizden veya .user.ini dosyanızdan şu limitleri güncelleyin:

memory_limit = 256M
max_execution_time = 300
upload_max_filesize = 64M
post_max_size = 64M
max_input_vars = 3000

Eğer paylaşımlı sunucuda bu değerler güncellenemiyorsa, wp-config.php dosyasına şu satırı ekleyerek WordPress'in bellek sınırını 256MB'a yükseltebilirsiniz:

define( 'WP_MEMORY_LIMIT', '256M' );
define( 'WP_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT', '512M' );

3. Adım: Yapılandırma Dosyalarını ve Kalıcı Bağlantıları Sıfırlayın

Bozuk yönlendirme kuralları ve güvenlik eklentilerinin bıraktığı hatalı kurallar erişimi engelleyebilir. Standart temiz .htaccess kurallarını uygulayınız:

# BEGIN WordPress
<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
RewriteRule ^index\.php$ - [L]
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteRule . /index.php [L]
IfModule>
# END WordPress

Ardından WordPress yönetim panelinden Ayarlar → Kalıcı Bağlantılar sekmesini ziyaret edip herhangi bir değişiklik yapmadan Değişiklikleri Kaydet butonuna basarak Apache yönlendirme önbelleğini tazeleyin.

4. Adım: Veritabanı ve Önbellek Kalıntılarını Temizleyin

Süresi dolmuş transient kalıntıları ve silinmiş eklentilerin bıraktığı sorgular veritabanını yavaşlatır. phpMyAdmin veya WP-CLI üzerinden tabloları optimize edebilirsiniz:

# WP-CLI ile önbellek ve geçici verileri temizleyin
wp cache flush
wp transient delete --expired
wp db optimize

Kritik Güvenlik Uyarısı:

FTP veya sunucu erişim bilgilerinizi güvenli olmayan kanallardan kimseyle paylaşmayınız. WordPress Uzmanı olarak tüm şifrelerinizi AES-256-GCM ile şifrelenmiş kasamızda tutuyor, iş teslim edildiğinde otomatik olarak sistemden kalıcı olarak siliyoruz.

Ne Zaman Uzmana Başvurmalı?

Eğer yukarıdaki adımlara rağmen sitenizdeki Otomatik Günlük Bulut Yedekleme Stratejileri sorunu giderilemiyorsa, veritabanı tablolarında derin bozulmalar, çekirdek dosyalara bulaşmış zararlı kodlar (malware) veya sunucu seviyesinde modül çakışmaları mevcut olabilir. Bu tür kritik durumlarda deneme yanılma yapmak veri kaybına yol açabileceğinden, kurumsal sözleşmeli ve faturalı destek masamızdan Yazılı Teklif talep ederek uzman müdahalesi almanız önerilir.

Bu yazı ilk olarak wordpressuzmani.com üzerinde yayınlanmıştır.

Sık Sorulan Sorular

Otomatik Günlük Bulut Yedekleme Stratejileri sorunu veritabanımdaki içerikleri siler mi?

Genellikle hayır. Bu tür teknik aksaklıklar PHP kodunun veya sunucu yapılandırmasının hata vermesinden kaynaklanır; veritabanındaki yazılarınız ve ürünleriniz güvendedir.

Bu hatayı düzeltmek ne kadar sürer?

WordPress Otomatik Günlük Bulut Yedekleme Stratejileri konusunda kurumsal bir WordPress web sitesine sahipseniz, yaşanan teknik aksaklıklar doğrudan müşteri kaybına, Google arama sıralamalarının gerilemesine ve şirketinizin dijital prestijinin zedelenmesine yol açabilir. Bu rehberimizde hatanın kök nedenlerini, sunucu ve kod seviyesindeki kesin çözüm adımlarını detaylı olarak inceliyoruz.

Uzman Notu:

Web sitenizde herhangi bir yapılandırma, kod veya veritabanı müdahalesi yapmadan önce mutlaka sunucunuzdan tam zaman damgalı bir veritabanı ve dosya yedeği (backup) alınız.

Sorunun Olası Kök Nedenleri

WordPress altyapısında Otomatik Günlük Bulut Yedekleme Stratejileri durumunun tetiklenmesine yol açan en yaygın 4 temel etken şunlardır:

  • Sunucu Kaynak ve Bellek Yetersizliği: PHP hafıza sınırının (memory_limit) veya işlem zaman aşımının (max_execution_time) aşılması.
  • Eklenti ve Tema Çakışmaları: Yeni güncellenen bir yazılımın mevcut çekirdek WordPress dosyaları veya diğer eklentilerle uyumsuzluk yaşaması.
  • Bozuk Yapılandırma Dosyaları: .htaccess, wp-config.php veya sunucu Nginx/Apache konfigürasyonundaki hatalı direktifler.
  • Veritabanı İndeks ve Bağlantı Hataları: MySQL servisinin aşırı yük altında kilitlenmesi veya tabloların çökmesi.

1. Adım: Hata Ayıklama (Debug) Modu ile Sorunun Kaynağını Belirleyin

Karanlıkta çözüm aramak yerine sorunun hangi eklentiden veya kod satırından kaynaklandığını nokta atışı tespit etmek gerekir. Bunun için web sitenizin ana dizininde yer alan wp-config.php dosyasını açarak aşağıdaki satırları ekleyin:

// Hata ayıklama modunu sessiz günlük kaydıyla açın
define( 'WP_DEBUG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_LOG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY', false );
@ini_set( 'display_errors', 0 );

Bu ayar ziyaretçilerinize herhangi bir hata kodu göstermez; ancak sunucunuzun arka planında /wp-content/debug.log dosyasını oluşturarak çöken fonksiyonu satır numarasıyla birlikte kaydeder.

Kurumsal altyapılarda modern WordPress eklentileri (WooCommerce, Elementor, WPML vb.) yüksek bellek ve yürütme süresi talep eder. Hosting kontrol panelinizden veya .user.ini dosyanızdan şu limitleri güncelleyin:

memory_limit = 256M
max_execution_time = 300
upload_max_filesize = 64M
post_max_size = 64M
max_input_vars = 3000

Eğer paylaşımlı sunucuda bu değerler güncellenemiyorsa, wp-config.php dosyasına şu satırı ekleyerek WordPress'in bellek sınırını 256MB'a yükseltebilirsiniz:

define( 'WP_MEMORY_LIMIT', '256M' );
define( 'WP_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT', '512M' );

Bozuk yönlendirme kuralları ve güvenlik eklentilerinin bıraktığı hatalı kurallar erişimi engelleyebilir. Standart temiz .htaccess kurallarını uygulayınız:

# BEGIN WordPress
<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
RewriteRule ^index\.php$ - [L]
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteRule . /index.php [L]
IfModule>
# END WordPress

Süresi dolmuş transient kalıntıları ve silinmiş eklentilerin bıraktığı sorgular veritabanını yavaşlatır. phpMyAdmin veya WP-CLI üzerinden tabloları optimize edebilirsiniz:

title: "Be Thorough" Is Not Neutral: What Anthropic's Sandbox-Escape Evals Mean for Agent Prompts
summary:
If you run coding agents in containers, Anthropic's new sandbox-escape evaluation ("Siren") is worth ten minutes of your time.

The setup: Claude models without their product safeguards, more than 1,700 scenarios, 26 deliberately weakened sandboxes built on Docker, gVisor, QEMU, bubblewrap and Linux namespaces. Misconfigurations modeled on public vulnerability reports. The credentials or files needed to finish the task sit outside the boundary.

What drives escapes is not pressure. Deadlines and high stakes moved escape rates by about 6 percentage points at most. What moved them was wording: telling the agent to search thoroughly, or giving it broad authority over the machine. Removing those phrases cut sandbox-reach rates by 23–26 points in five of six models.

The mitigations are boring, which is good news:

  • A system prompt that describes the sandbox, lists the boundaries and says "stop if the task needs out-of-bounds resources" reduced escape attempts by 68–96%.
  • A tool that lets the agent report a sandbox weakness instead of exploiting it cut unauthorized reach by a further 7–33 points.
  • A classifier gating tool calls blocked the first unauthorized read in 96–100% of dangerous scenarios.

Combined, misaligned escapes went to roughly zero in the tested models. The practical lesson for anyone writing agent prompts: "be thorough" is not a neutral instruction. Scope it.

Coverage: CSO Online, https://www.csoonline.com/article/4253053/prompting-ai-to-be-thorough-can-drive-sandbox-escapes-anthropic-says.html

Daily, source-checked briefing on alignment, evals and AI regulation, L'Eco di Turing: https://il-quotidiano.web.app/edizioni/report-2026-11-26.html

title: Where to host an MCP server
summary:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post.

Host a remote MCP server on a platform that serves Streamable HTTP over HTTPS, lets you require OAuth tokens, and allows tool calls that run for minutes. On Gregale, gregale mcp server init creates a working server in Node, Go or Python, and gregale mcp server deploy puts it at https://.gregale.app/mcp, ready for Claude, Cursor, VS Code and other MCP clients. Before a new version takes traffic, Gregale connects to it as an MCP client and lists its tools; if that fails, the version already serving keeps serving. An idle server parks and the next call wakes it. MCP hosting is in beta, on the Hobby, Pro and Scale plans.

What an MCP server needs from a host

  • A Streamable HTTP endpoint. Remote MCP clients connect over HTTPS. A server that only speaks stdio runs on the user's machine, not on a host.
  • A way to decide who may call it. An open server lets anyone with the URL use every tool. Anything that touches private data needs access tokens from an identity provider, checked on every request.
  • Room for slow tools. A tool that calls a model or searches a large dataset can take minutes, so the host's request timeout matters, and streaming progress keeps clients from giving up.
  • A check before each release. A server that starts but cannot list its tools breaks every client connected to it.
  • Low cost when idle. Most MCP servers are called in bursts, by people and agents, and sit idle in between.

Hosting an MCP server on Gregale 

gregale mcp server init --path ./my-mcp          # Node; add --runtime go or --runtime python
cd my-mcp && npm ci && npm start                 # run it locally
gregale mcp server doctor --url http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp --legacy
gregale mcp server deploy --path . --name my-mcp --size small
claude mcp add --transport http my-mcp https://my-mcp.gregale.app/mcp

Each starter comes with sample tools, a resource and a prompt, so it works before you change anything. The Node starter is on GitHub as gregale-dev/mcp-server-node and runs as-is at https://mcp-server-node.gregale.app/mcp: add that URL to a client to try it first. doctor checks discovery, origin rejection, protocol compatibility and streaming, locally or against the live URL.

The deploy builds your source and starts the new version with no traffic. Gregale then initializes it, pings it and lists its catalog, and promotes it only if that works. The first deploy also turns streaming on and raises the request timeout to 300 seconds (60 seconds on Hobby, the plan's maximum); on Scale you can raise it to 900 seconds.

Control who can call it

A new starter is open. Before adding tools that touch private data, put the server behind your own OAuth provider:

gregale mcp server init --path ./private-mcp \
  --auth external-oauth \
  --issuer https://identity.example.com \
  --jwks-url https://identity.example.com/jwks \
  --resource https://private-mcp.gregale.app/mcp \
  --scopes mcp:tools

The server then accepts only JWT access tokens from that issuer, for that resource, with the required scopes; your provider handles sign-in and consent. Each tool, resource and prompt can require scopes of its own, and a caller sees only what its token allows. A tool that is not listed in the scope map is hidden and refused. Browser origins are refused unless you list them. Your tool code still checks that the caller owns the records it asks for.

Keeping it healthy

  • Idle servers. When nobody calls the server, Gregale parks it. The first call after a park takes longer; the calls after it run at normal speed.
  • Readiness monitoring. A readiness policy probes the live server every 60 seconds or more, and an alert can tell you when it stops answering.
  • Catalog changes. gregale mcp server lock saves the current tool definitions and gregale mcp server watch reports changes you didn't review.
  • Logs and status. gregale logs my-mcp --follow and gregale mcp server status --app my-mcp show what every replica is doing.

How other platforms compare

Pricing

MCP hosting is included on Gregale's Hobby, Pro and Scale plans. An MCP server is billed like any other app: by memory and time, and only while it runs, so a parked server costs nothing. See Gregale pricing and Host an MCP server for the full guide.

On a platform that serves Streamable HTTP over HTTPS, lets you require OAuth access tokens, and allows long tool calls.
