Can an MCP server scale to zero on Gregale?

Yes. When nobody calls the server, Gregale parks it and stops billing; the next call wakes it. The first call after a park takes longer, and the calls after it run at normal speed.

How do I keep an MCP server private?

Create it with --auth external-oauth and your provider's issuer and JWKS URL. The server then accepts only JWT access tokens from that issuer with the required scopes, and each tool can require scopes of its own.

title: Why Read-Only Database Access Matters More Than You Think
summary:
Why Read-Only Database Access Matters More Than You Think

The first question every engineering lead asks when someone proposes letting non-technical teammates query a production database is some version of: what happens if they break something?

It's the right question. And it's the one that decides whether a self-service data tool ever gets turned on for anyone outside engineering.

TL;DR

Read-only enforcement is what makes natural-language database querying safe to hand to non-engineers. Query1AI generates and executes SELECT statements only — write operations aren't a configuration someone could disable, they're simply not in the execution path. Try it free →

The Real Risk Isn't Bad Questions — It's Write Access

Someone who doesn't know SQL asking a confusing question isn't actually dangerous. Worst case, they get an answer that doesn't match what they meant, and they ask again more precisely. That's a UX problem, not a safety problem.

The actual risk shows up the moment a tool sitting between a person and a production database is capable of more than reading. A natural-language interface that can also run UPDATE, DELETE, or DDL statements turns every ambiguous question into a potential incident — not because anyone intended harm, but because a misread intent plus write access is how rows get modified or dropped by accident.

This is also the reason most teams never seriously consider giving broader database access to non-engineers in the first place. It isn't that the questions aren't reasonable. It's that the access model doesn't give anyone confidence nothing will go wrong.

Read-Only Has to Be Structural, Not a Setting

There's a meaningful difference between a tool that's configured to avoid write operations and one that's incapable of them.

A configuration is a setting someone could change, a permission someone could misconfigure, or a default that quietly shifts in a future update. It depends on someone remembering it's there.

An architectural constraint doesn't depend on anyone remembering anything. If the query execution layer only knows how to run SELECT statements — if INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and DDL simply aren't operations the system is able to send to the database — then there's no scenario where a misinterpreted question becomes a destructive one. Not because it's discouraged. Because it isn't possible.

How This Shows Up in Query1AI

1DataCloud's Query1AI is built around exactly this constraint. It takes a plain-English question, reads the schema metadata the Unified Dashboard already mapped for that database — table names, column names, data types, relationships — and turns the question into SQL. That SQL is read-only by construction: Query1AI generates and executes SELECT statements, and nothing else is in its vocabulary.

That means a sales rep asking "which customers haven't logged in for 30 days" and a product manager asking a question that gets parsed in a way they didn't expect both land in the same place: a query that reads data and returns it. Neither one can accidentally trigger a write, because the path from question to query never passes through write operations at all.

The generated SQL is also visible before and after it runs. If a result looks off, the actual query is right there to check — nothing about how the answer was produced is hidden from the person who asked.

Why This Changes What's Possible for a Team

Once read-only is a structural guarantee rather than a policy, the conversation about who gets database access changes shape entirely.

Engineers stop being the only safe option. When write access was on the table, restricting database access to engineers was the responsible choice. When it isn't on the table, that restriction is solving a problem that no longer exists.

Self-service stops being a risk tradeoff. Letting a product manager or a sales lead query a database directly isn't "convenience traded against safety" anymore — the safety constraint doesn't loosen just because more people have access.

Mistakes stay cheap. A confusing question produces a confusing answer, which gets refined and asked again. It never produces a changed row, a dropped table, or a corrupted dataset.

What Read-Only Doesn't Mean

Worth being precise here: read-only means the query execution path can only read data — it doesn't mean every table or column is automatically appropriate for every person to see.
